Questurian / analytical field guide / 7 September 2026

What happens between
the seed and the article?

A plain-English study of Prompt2Blog: what each step receives, what it changes, what the next step assumes, and why a technically completed run can still produce a strange article.

Current code tracedSaved runs inspectedExact prompts includedNo proposed fixes
01 · The whole journey02 · What travels between steps03 · Decide the article04 · Find and choose material05 · Write, inspect, edit, choose06 · Who instructs the writer?07 · Instruction tensions08 · Follow a real run09 · Where the work goes10 · After the graph11 · Prompt reading room12 · Evidence and limits13 · Source snapshots

01 / The whole journey

FindingPrompt2Blog repeatedly translates an article idea before it writes a sentence. The interview becomes a brief. The brief becomes questions. Search answers become fact records. Those records become a shortlist. The shortlist becomes a writing packet. The packet becomes a section plan. Only then does a model write prose. Other calls inspect and sometimes change that prose.

That complexity is real. Calling it “overengineered” is a judgment about whether the benefit is worth the cost; this report does not assume that conclusion. What the code demonstrates is that the final writer is one participant in a chain of decisions. A strange result may start several steps earlier, and a later pass can reward compliance with a decision that was wrong for the article.

01 →Seed → grillLook up the topic; interview the operator. 02 →Brief → work orderDefine the article; translate it into research questions. 03 →Search → dossierGather cited notes; turn them into structured claims. 04 →Gate → selectionDecide whether research is sufficient; choose facts. 05 →Packet → outlineFreeze material; plan sections and reader payoffs. 06 →Compose → cleanupWrite the article; optionally edit style errors. 07 →Ground → auditCheck against records; score the draft and flag work. 08 →Repair → settleOptionally edit once, recheck, choose a draft, save.
The loop: audit → repair → optional style cleanup → groundedness → audit → settle. One automatic repair attempt. Settle may restore the earlier draft.

Three different meanings of success: “completed” means an artifact was saved; “grounded” means the checker found no high-severity unsupported claims; “ready_for_staging” means the configured readiness checks passed. None means a human enjoyed reading it. A completed article can carry needs_revision.

The current writing graph has seven named nodes, including optional repair. It has no separate title node. The v3 names on current writing files and saved stages do not establish an alternative v3 intake: v4 intake feeds this graph. topology_v3.py:1 finalize.py:46

02 / What travels between steps

An “artifact” here simply means a saved piece of work. Most artifacts are structured records, not prose. A claim ID is a label connecting a fact to later decisions; a fingerprint is a checksum that detects whether an input changed.

ObjectIn ordinary wordsContents / what the next step expects
SeedThe operator’s opening line.Starts the run. Current finalization keeps it as the title; it can therefore contain a promise the body must justify.
Grill stateThe interview notebook.Seed, lookup digest and URLs, questions, recommendations, answers, covered markers, consensus. The brief builder expects an agreed interview.
Article BriefWhat this article is supposed to be.Location, form, reader, reader question, outcome, spine, must_name, supplied material, fails_if. It remains available downstream; “never consumed” means it is not thrown away after planning.
Work OrderWhat research must answer.Primary subject and scope; reference roles; assumptions; separately identified questions with purpose, kind, precision and search group. It is a model’s translation of the brief.
Gathered notesSearch results written up by a model.Narrative answers plus returned source URLs, indexed by question. These are already a synthesis, not a bundle of untouched web pages.
EvidencePackage / dossierThe research filing cabinet.Sources, claim texts, links from claims to sources and questions, dates/confidence, question verdicts, assumptions, conflicts and gaps.
SelectionThe editorial cut.Merged IDs, ranked order, reasons and roles, keep count, texture reserve, rescued and dropped facts. It can change without deleting the dossier.
WritingPacketWhat is laid on this writer’s desk.Chosen claims copied verbatim, attached limitations/conflicts, operator notes, supplied material and fingerprints. Built by code; frozen at writing.
Stage contextsDifferent views for different jobs.The outline, compose, audit and repair each receive a different assembled instruction package. “The prompt” is not one file.
OutlineThe intended reading sequence.Headings, reader_payoff, claim IDs, word budgets, answer focus and unsupported requests. Code validates it before passing a plan onward.
Rewrite + reviewsThe draft and its inspections.Article body plus internal gaps; grounding verdict; quality scores and revisions; deterministic checks. More than one draft can exist during repair.
Final artifactThe chosen version and receipt.Title, Markdown, brief, work order, packet receipt, scores, flags, repair outcome, model/cost records and optional debug prompts.

The most consequential separation is dossier ≠ packet. Groundedness can read the full dossier while the writer only receives the selected packet. A researched fact can be absent from the draft because it was cut, because the outline did not place it, or because compose chose not to use it. Those are different causes. packet_v4.py:1 instructions_v3.py:548

03 / Decide the article

A · Saved state + web model

Open a run and research the seed

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
The typed seed.Creates a run ID before the interview finishes. A grounded call asks for a few dense paragraphs about facts, reputation, neighbourhoods and what the subject is known for. The result and source URLs enter the interview notebook. Lookup failure can leave the interview running without that digest.A saved run and an initial research digest.

Next step expects: The grill uses that digest to avoid asking the operator questions it could look up.

Watch point: This search prepares the interview. It is not the later evidence dossier; a fact influencing the brief can need researching again. intake.py:160 grill_v4.py:173

B · Model each turn; optional extra web calls

Grill: ask, recommend, record, repeat

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Seed, accumulated research, full interview transcript, covered/missing brief markers and remaining lookup allowance.The model chooses one question, drafts a recommended answer, can push back, and tracks whether the brief’s markers are covered. Accepting a suggested answer counts as answering. It can request up to three mid-interview lookups in addition to the first search. Turns repeat until the required markers are filled and consensus is returned.A question to show the operator, or an agreed summary. Every turn is saved.

Next step expects: The brief builder expects enough agreement to populate all required fields.

Watch point: The recommendations themselves supply editorial judgment. When an operator accepts them, part of the “approved intent” originated with the model. The code records that distinction in the grill transcript, but the brief prompt presents question-and-answer text without the same accepted-draft annotations. grill_v4.py:295 brief_v4.py:109

C · Structured model call; validation / retry handling

Build the Article Brief

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Interview answers, consensus, seed and the form catalog’s allowed choices/exclusions.Converts conversational intent into a structured commission. It chooses a form and infers unspecified fields from what was said. Supplied personal material must point back to exact answers; code validates that provenance. The resulting brief receives a fingerprint.A saved Article Brief. This is an additional model transformation after the interview.

Next step expects: Planning treats its spine, outcome, must-name list and failure definition as the article’s obligations.

Watch point: “Every field must carry a real value” creates pressure to decide what the interview left uncertain. The brief may be more specific than the operator’s own contribution. Current prompt also says the seed is not a promise, contrary to later stages. brief_v4.py:109

D · Structured model call; operator can cut

Translate the brief into a Work Order

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Brief, the seed as headline, and a length-derived estimate of how many facts the article can hold.Writes questions with a purpose, load-bearing/texture kind, exact/approximate precision and optional shared search group. Also defines assumptions and scope roles. The operator can strike questions or add questions; adding one marks it load-bearing. Code removes assumptions no longer referenced after a cut.Research questions plus scope and budget projection. Cutting is deterministic; planning is an AI call.

Next step expects: Research needs questions that can be answered independently, with named geography and no placeholders awaiting an earlier answer.

Watch point: One idea can become many separate obligations. “One question, one fact” pushes toward splitting; length guidance pushes toward restraint. A default of exact precision and load-bearing operator additions can make ordinary editorial preferences into pre-writing blockers. work_order_v4.py:175

Before research starts, code can refuse a plan projected beyond the token ceiling or one with no texture question. The familiar phrase “one gate” describes the editorial design; it does not mean the program has only one refusal condition. Validation, credentials, budget and stale-input checks can also stop work. work_order_v4.py:933 intake_v4.py:412

04 / Find and choose material

E · Grounded web model; up to four concurrent requests

Gather cited research notes

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Location and each question’s wording/precision. The full editorial brief, voice and word budget are not included in the single-question gather prompt.Questions sharing search_group are combined, at most four per request. Ungrouped questions run separately. Each embedded question says “Answer it as fully as you can, with sources. Then keep going,” and asks for names, hours, prices and interesting side discoveries. The grouped wrapper asks for concise facts and no repeated background. Completed notes are checkpointed for reuse.Narrative notes and URLs. For a grouped request, each question initially points to the same shared response; token counts are not multiplied per question.

Next step expects: The structurer must assign the relevant pieces of those notes to the correct question and source.

Watch point: There is a direct expansion pressure: the planner is told to buy only what fits, but the researcher is told to continue beyond the question. Grouping reduces repeated retrieval; it does not remove that instruction. research_v4.py:802 research_v4.py:1027

F · Model calls in batches of four questions; code merges

Structure notes into the dossier

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Each batch’s question IDs, kinds and precision, saved notes and compact source URL handles.A model extracts sources and distinct claims, links claims to questions, and assigns supported/partial/missing/unpublished/nonexistent verdicts as applicable. It is told to add nothing outside the notes and that two or three claims usually answer a question. Code normalizes data, restores exact URLs, namespaces IDs and merges duplicate sources. Successful batches are cached by their input fingerprints.An EvidencePackage with fact records and question verdicts.

Next step expects: Later stages treat these claim texts as the factual reference record.

Watch point: This is an important trust boundary: the record is a model’s extraction of a model’s search synthesis. A correct schema and a valid source ID do not prove that a claim faithfully represents the original page. research_v4.py:1240 research_v4.py:1585

G · Additional model call; deterministic reconciliation

Check assumptions and cross-question conflicts

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Declared assumptions and the assembled claim IDs/texts.Assesses assumptions and names disagreements between claims. This cross-batch call sees claim texts, rather than the full gathered notes and web pages. Code reconciles the returned verdicts and links.Premise findings and conflict records attached to the dossier.

Next step expects: Coverage uses refuted assumptions to decide whether writing can start; the packet carries conflicts relevant to selected facts.

Watch point: The prompt asks for a resolution “where the notes settled” a disagreement, but this prompt passes claim texts. Unless that resolution survived in those texts, the checker is being asked to recover context it does not receive. research_v4.py:1301

H · Deterministic editorial gate

Decide whether there is enough to write

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
The whole dossier and the work order.Load-bearing questions must be settled: supported, unpublished or nonexistent. A recorded refuted assumption blocks. At least one texture question must be supported or partial. The gate does not ask a fresh model whether the piece will be enjoyable.can_write plus named gaps. Operator actions can answer, omit or re-ask questions, resolve an assumption, and handle venue facts. Changes trigger coverage again and create or rebind selection when eligible.

Next step expects: Writing requires this verdict to pass, and also requires a usable selection.

Watch point: “Has texture” means an appropriately labelled question has an accepted status. It is a proxy for interesting material, not a judgment of interest. A settled unpublished answer can clear a requirement while giving the writer nothing it may say about that missing fact. coverage_v4.py:78 intake_v4.py:528

I · Up to four selection model passes

Deduplicate, fold, rank and reserve texture

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Dossier; the ranking passes also receive brief/work-order context appropriate to their job.First merges repeated claims. Then folds facts repeated once per item. Then ranks survivors for this article, with reasons and roles. Texture is ranked separately and gets a 20% reserve. The initial keep count is length-derived: about two claims per 100 words, minimum eight. The operator can change the line, rescue or drop facts.A separate selection record. At 900 words, the usual starting line is 18 claims; it is not an absolute cap.

Next step expects: The packet builder needs known selected IDs and matching input fingerprints.

Watch point: Selection is an editorial judgment and can discard a useful fact. If ranking fails, current code keeps all surviving claims and records a warning. That differs from a completely missing selection, which refuses writing. One can still reach a very large packet through the failure path. selection_v4.py:1095

J · Code only; no model paraphrase

Freeze the writing packet

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Brief, dossier and current selection.Copies selected facts verbatim with their dates/confidence, linked source notes, conflicts and operator notes. Supplied material comes from the brief. IDs/fingerprints guard the handoff. The resulting packet is frozen into the runtime request for writing and resume.A narrower view of research plus separate stage instructions.

Next step expects: Outline and compose may use only this material. Groundedness continues to have the whole dossier.

Watch point: This step protects against another paraphrase, but cannot undo meaning already lost during research extraction or selection. The coverage gate checked the whole dossier before the cut; a passed gate does not establish that every brief obligation remains supported inside the chosen packet. packet_v4.py:1 intake_v4.py:1135

05 / Write, inspect, edit, choose

K · One model call, then code validation

Outline the article

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Voice, brief, audience, form excerpts, selected facts/roles, structural rules and section word budget.Returns headings, reader payoffs, claims and word allocations. Code checks the plan’s structure, scope, claims and other constraints. It may drop invalid context-only sections. An unusable plan degrades to answer/takeaway focus without sections; a recoverable outline failure does not stop compose.An accepted section plan or a focus-only/empty plan, plus diagnostics.

Next step expects: Compose is told to follow the section plan when present; without it, the writer must invent the structure from the remaining inputs.

Watch point: Planning can cost a full call and still supply no sections. The user sees a pipeline with an outline stage, but that does not prove the article was written from an accepted outline. outline.py:35

L · Structured prose-producing model call

Compose the article

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Outline, selected packet, voice, brief, form, topic modules, audience, conventions, house rules, length/style directive, SEO block and full anti-AI block.Returns article Markdown inside JSON, a suggested title, alignment statement, improvements and remaining gaps. Code sanitizes that response. The final title still comes from the seed, even though this output schema asks for improved_title.The first article body and internal metadata. Then style validation runs immediately.

Next step expects: Grounding will compare what this writer actually said with the saved research, not trust the writer’s claims of compliance.

Watch point: The writer is managing many independent obligations at once. “Use every must-name item,” “invent nothing,” “make a clear judgment,” and “follow the plan” can be impossible to satisfy together when an earlier transformation left a gap. compose.py:1

M · Free validator; conditional model edit

Clean up style errors

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Draft plus deterministic style errors mapped to sections, and the repair lock.If valid, makes no call. Otherwise sends only identifiable affected sections, with their IDs and text hashes. One model attempt edits them. Unknown/off-target replacements are discarded. The change is kept only if it reduces counted style errors. Document-wide errors that cannot be placed can remain.The draft after cleanup, or the unchanged draft with a report explaining why.

Next step expects: Groundedness checks the resulting draft afterward.

Watch point: The cleanup prompt says the prose has “already [been] checked for accuracy,” but on the compose path this occurs before the first grounding check. Also, fewer style errors is the acceptance test; it is not a direct semantic comparison proving every fact was preserved. style_cleanup.py:68 compose.py:13

N · Model reads article against full research records

Check groundedness

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Draft title/body, full evidence records, supplied material and evidence-disposition rules.Flags unsupported statements and overclaims, checking dates, geography, confidence and unresolved conflicts. It accepts general background and judgments under stated exceptions. It does not independently revisit every web page.checked, grounded, assessment and quoted unsupported claims labelled high or low severity.

Next step expects: Audit treats this verdict as authoritative on factual support.

Watch point: grounded=true explicitly allows low-severity unsupported claims. A fact-extraction error that has already entered the dossier can also look supported here. Grounding is primarily a consistency check against the research record. editorial_v3.py:142 groundedness.py:1

O · Model assessment + deterministic measurements

Audit quality and measure constraints

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Draft, brief/promise/fails-if, form and audience, compact support context, grounding verdict, measured checks and section promises.The model scores utility and fidelity, quotes a fails-if violation if present, and lists required revisions/unresolved section payoffs. Code separately counts words and checks configured constraints, and prepares the repair decision.A review and a route to repair or settle. The readiness score threshold is 7; other checks also matter.

Next step expects: Repair needs specific revisions it can map to existing sections.

Watch point: The rubric defines 7–8 as acceptable with edits, so a passing score is not a finished editorial standard. The audit can only evaluate section promises that survived planning. Counts and model scores can dominate a reader’s experience of the prose. editorial_v3.py:219 quality.py:26

P · Conditional model edit + repeat groundedness/audit

Repair once, then recheck

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Current article, required revisions, flagged statements, section map/hashes, editable targets, selected facts and an immutable scope/style lock.Returns replacements for existing sections. It can use selected facts compose omitted, but cannot add/delete/reorder sections. Code validates IDs, hashes, allowed facts and scope. Style cleanup may run again, then grounding and audit repeat. A repair can be refused because the draft passed, its one attempt was spent, or the projected monetary repair budget is exceeded.A candidate revised article and a fresh assessment.

Next step expects: Settle compares the original and candidate, not merely whichever came last.

Watch point: An audit may identify a structural problem that section replacement cannot perform. A revision that cannot be localized may broaden the allowed target set. “Scoped repair” limits changes, but still includes the previous article and selected facts in its prompt, so it is not necessarily a small input. audit_repair.py:292 repair_targets.py:1

Q · Code only

Settle and finalize

ReceivesWhat happensProduces / next expectation
Draft candidates with their grounding, checks and quality scores.Ranks grounding first, then fewer readiness blockers, overall score, brief-coverage score and finally distance from the length band. It keeps the best-ranked version; equal ranking does not require replacing the original. Finalization uses the seed title, combines it with the body, saves the artifact and marks the run completed.Final Markdown plus ready_for_staging or needs_revision, quality review and usage receipt.

Next step expects: An operator reads and decides what to save or stage. The quality stamp is advisory.

Watch point: A paid repair may be discarded. The latest grounding stage row can then describe the rejected candidate, while the final artifact contains the earlier draft’s verdict. Studying only the last stage row can explain the wrong article. policies.py:105 audit_repair.py:467

06 / Who instructs the writer?

The compose prompt is assembled at runtime. Editing a voice file changes only one part of it. JSON schemas also instruct the model by defining which fields it must return. The following map describes the current code; the exact historical assembled prompt in the reading room shows what one saved run received.

LayerJobWhere it enters
Stage templateDefines task, output JSON and hard rules.Outline, compose, groundedness, audit or repair template.
Authority orderEvidence → brief → form → topic modules → audience → house style.Outline, compose and audit contexts.
Questurian VoiceAdult, unsold, attentive, opinionated, direct.Outline and compose contexts.
Brief + work-order scopeSubject, outcome, spine, must-name, fails-if and allowed reference roles.Different representations in planning, writing, judging and repair.
Facts and limitationsThe permitted factual material.Packet for outline/compose/repair; full records for groundedness; compact support context for audit.
FormHow this type of article opens, divides and ends.Structured form policy plus selected prose sections from its Markdown file.
Topic modules + audienceEmphasis for the topic and intended reader.Compose gets active topic modules; outline/audit have narrower context sets.
Writing conventions + house rulesDates, prices, attribution, headings, evidence discipline and reader service.Compose receives both; audit and repair see different subsets/locks.
Length directiveWord target, band and prose guidance.Compose, audit and repair style directive; also outline budget.
SEO-safe rulesDirect answer near top, takeaways at end and natural keywords.Unconditionally inserted into compose.
ANTI_AI_TELLS_FULLBanned shapes/words, sentence rhythm, specificity and punctuation.Appended after the assembled compose prompt; declares overriding authority.
Style cleanup rulesInstructions for replacing only sections with detected errors.Separate conditional model call, not a mere formatting operation.

instructions_v3.py:548 compose.py:1 anti_ai_tells.py:35

The writer has more than one voice authority.

The single Questurian voice file exists. Alongside it, the shared anti-AI block contains its own “Voice rules,” examples, and an explicit statement that it overrides conflicting instructions above. “One voice file” therefore does not mean one source of prose direction.

07 / Instruction tensions worth marking

These are observations to study, not a repair plan. Observed means the code or saved result directly shows it. Risk means the instructions plausibly create pressure toward a failure; this report does not claim to have measured the causal effect.

Observed conflict

Two competing authority orders

The compose context puts verified evidence first. The anti-AI header says “override any conflicting instruction above.” Its disclaimer section says “Do not caveat a fact,” while the evidence rules demand preserving consequential limits. Later sentences qualify that ban, but the writer must reconcile two different top-level authorities.

instructions_v3.py:31 anti_ai_tells.py:35
Observed conflict

The seed stops binding, then becomes binding again

The brief builder labels it “provenance only — it is not a promise to keep.” The work-order prompt calls it the headline the article will be published under. Finalization uses it unchanged apart from dash normalization. A successfully refined brief can leave a mismatched headline intact.

brief_v4.py:109 work_order_v4.py:175
Observed conflict

Form-specific structure meets universal SEO structure

The current form policy can choose different openings and endings. Compose still receives an SEO block demanding one direct 40–60 word answer and closing key takeaways. The outline planning context also describes opening/takeaways as items it does not plan. These directives do not all adapt to the form together.

generation.py:4 instructions_v3.py:658
Observed pressure

Buy less, then keep researching

Work-order length guidance constrains editorial room. The gather prompt asks for a full answer and then interesting things nobody asked about. A grouped wrapper asks for concision while repeating that expansion instruction for each question. Research can grow faster than the article’s needs.

research_v4.py:802
Observed boundary

A useful research answer can become unsayable

Coverage considers unpublished answers settled. The disposition policy requires the article to omit unpublished facts silently. That may be coherent for a missing statistic, but leaves pressure when the brief still demands a practical answer or a concrete mention tied to it.

coverage_v4.py:42 instructions_v3.py:95
Risk

“Interesting” is represented by labels

The gate’s has_texture is true when at least one texture question has supported or partial status. It does not measure whether those claims are vivid, relevant or enjoyable. The reader-facing meaning of “nothing worth reading” is broader than what the test actually checks.

coverage_v4.py:111
Observed boundary

The checker’s pass permits unsupported details

grounded=true means no high-severity unsupported claims. Low-severity claims remain visible in the review. The general instruction “delete unsupported assertions” is stricter than the boolean used in readiness. The latest final article demonstrates that difference.

editorial_v3.py:197
Risk

A mandatory list can outrun the available evidence

Compose must name every must_name item, keep an exact scope, hit a length and invent nothing. If selection omitted required support, or the brief asks for an unresearched detail, those commands cannot all be satisfied. The model may omit the obligation, generalize a narrower fact, or invent a detail.

editorial_v3.py:103
Observed asymmetry

Research has information that the writer cannot see

Coverage and groundedness use the whole dossier. Compose sees the packet. A passing research gate is therefore not a direct check of the exact set the writer receives. Conversely, grounding can support a claim from outside the editorial cut without identifying it as a selection violation.

intake_v4.py:1135 groundedness.py:1
Risk

Anti-AI rules can produce an artificial rhythm of their own

The shared rules require every section to have a sentence under eight words and one over twenty-five, aggressively break clusters, ration compounds and put specific anchors in paragraphs. These are explicit patterns the writer must perform. Their presence does not establish that the resulting prose sounds natural.

anti_ai_tells.py:194
Observed mismatch

A cleanup pass assumes an earlier accuracy check

The cleanup template says accuracy has already been checked. Compose invokes cleanup before groundedness. Its acceptance criterion counts style errors; a reduced count can coexist with semantic drift, which is only checked later against the dossier.

style_cleanup.py:68
Observed drift

Prompts still carry explanations of old failures as current truth

The punch-list prompt says nothing in the system has ever read fails_if, but the quality audit now reads and quotes it. Work-order text says every question is researched alone while the gather code now groups related questions. These statements are not reliable descriptions of the current program.

notes_v4.py:228 research_v4.py:1003

08 / Follow a real run: Valparaíso’s hill elevators

This is the newest saved normal Prompt2Blog run found in the local database, created 6 September 2026. It is historical evidence: it does not prove that every prompt in today’s checkout was used on that run. The claims below are comparisons within the saved record, not fresh travel advice or independent verification of opening hours.

e001d48c-9881-4d30-8250-002b5a33ff31

7 → 165 → 34Saved work-order questions → dossier claims → packet facts
37Recorded calls across the run, including repeated work
922 wordsFinal measured body; 900 target; needs_revision

1. The title and brief are already pointing at different prices

Valparaiso built thirty hill elevators to get people home, most of the network is dead, and the handful still running are the best two hundred pesos you will spend in the city.

The brief explicitly asks for a visitor fare of 1,000 pesos beside a resident fare of 200. The saved final body follows that distinction. The final title still promises “the best two hundred pesos you will spend.” This is a mismatch visible without judging the prose’s quality or checking an external source.

One fact, across the handoff

Research questionStructured claimFinal prose
What is the standard visitor fare in Chilean pesos for a single ride on a hill elevator (ascensor) in Valparaíso, Chile?The fare for foreign tourists on ascensores in Valparaíso, Chile, is $1,000 CLP per trip, effective January 2, 2026.The fare for foreign tourists is 1,000 pesos per trip, set on 2 January 2026.

The question requests a fare; the research record adds a date and links to two sources; the selected claim ID is present in the packet receipt; compose turns the same information into a sentence without source attribution. Notice that the claim’s as_of field is null even though its text contains a date. The date survives here because it remains in the claim text. This is the kind of record-to-prose transformation the pipeline is built around.

Exact structured claim record

2. The original research became a much larger filing cabinet

The saved work order contains seven questions and the saved dossier contains 165 claims. This is not a clean one-pass conversion rate: research has five recorded stage attempts, and the record includes operator settlements. The important observed size is the material actually present when this run reached writing. Selection started with keep_count=18 but has saved rescues/drops, yielding 34 packet facts. Those adjustments are visible; this report does not attribute every adjustment to a particular person or tool.

3. The paid outline was not used as a section plan

The candidate had six sections totalling 735 planned words. Its recorded checks passed section count, unique headings, word budget, claim IDs and context-only scope, but covers_primary_subject=false. The accepted outline’s sections list is empty. Compose received focus text and wrote its own structure. The compose result explicitly reports that no usable section plan was supplied.

4. A requirement was missing from the facts

The brief asks whether there is somewhere to sit at every named working ascensor. The initial compose metadata says the evidence does not establish that. In the later repair candidate, the checker flags assertions such as “There is room to sit on the promenade” and “Neither top has anywhere to sit” as unsupported. This is the shape of an impossible handoff: the obligation remains, but the material needed to satisfy it is missing.

5. The repair happened, then the earlier draft won

Settle records one repair attempt, a final score of 6, a last score of 6, and reverted_to_earlier_draft=true. That means the final article is not simply the last thing a model wrote. The pipeline spent work on the candidate and then kept the earlier version under its ranking policy.

6. “Grounded” still has exceptions in the chosen final draft

The final artifact’s own grounding review has zero high-severity findings, so grounded is true. It nevertheless lists three low-severity unsupported statements. One is “Both keep the standard hours.” The review explains that the record gives San Agustín a 21:00 closing, different from the general 21:30 schedule. This does not establish the real opening time; it establishes that the saved review noticed a mismatch and still returned its passing boolean.

The run is completed, but the final artifact is needs_revision, with overall score 6. This is not evidence that the system silently declared the whole article good. It shows that the system can complete, identify defects, attempt a repair, reject that repair, and still hand over a flawed article as designed.

# Valparaiso built thirty hill elevators to get people home, most of the network is dead, and the handful still running are the best two hundred pesos you will spend in the city.

Valparaíso built its hill elevators as transit for the people living up the slopes. Most of that network no longer runs. What survives is enough for one afternoon on foot.

Seven of Valparaíso's roughly thirty ascensores were confirmed running in June 2026. A foreign visitor pays 1,000 pesos a trip; a resident pays 200. Of the seven, El Peral, Concepción, Reina Victoria and Espíritu Santo put you somewhere at the top worth the climb in a single afternoon.

## What a ride costs

The fare for foreign tourists is 1,000 pesos per trip, set on 2 January 2026. Residents pay a general fare of 200 pesos over the same period, while children under 14, students with valid accreditation and anyone over 60 ride free. Ascensor Concepción is the exception: its resident fare is 300 pesos rather than 200, though a foreign visitor still pays 1,000 there. Ascensor Barón charges 600 pesos to carry a bicycle, as of 28 February 2026. You buy each trip at the station window, so four rides come to 4,000 pesos for a visitor. A visitor pays five times the general resident fare. The split is deliberate, and it is part of what the ascensores now are.

## Which ascensores are running

As of June 2026, seven were operational: Barón, Concepción, Cordillera, El Peral, Reina Victoria, Espíritu Santo and San Agustín. That fits the broader tally from October 2025, when 7 of the 16 protected historical elevators were in service. Most run Monday to Friday from 07:00 to 21:30, and Saturday, Sunday and public holidays from 08:00 to 21:30. Concepción keeps nearly the same hours, opening at 07:00 on weekdays and 08:00 at weekends and on public holidays, and closing at 21:30 throughout. The working list shifts without warning. Check each one is moving before you build a route around it.

## El Peral, up to Cerro Alegre

Start at El Peral. Its upper station opens onto Paseo Yugoslavo, a promenade on Cerro Alegre with wide views over the bay and the mountains standing behind the city. The Museo Municipal de Bellas Artes de Valparaíso sits on the promenade itself. It is the natural place to begin, because one ride puts you on the promenade with the museum at hand and the ridge walk toward Concepción starting from the same spot. A visitor pays 1,000 pesos. Weekday hours are 07:00 to 21:30, with a later 08:00 start at weekends and on holidays.

## Concepción and Reina Victoria, along the ridge

From Paseo Yugoslavo, follow the ridge to Cerro Concepción and Paseo Gervasoni, the top of Ascensor Concepción. Concepción opened in 1883 and is the oldest ascensor in the city, and it was confirmed running in May and June 2026. Paseo Gervasoni looks out over the port, and the streets around it are lined with painted houses, cafés and restaurants. A visitor pays 1,000 pesos here, the resident fare 300.

Then Reina Victoria. Its upper station sits on Pasaje Dimalow, and the exit opens into Plaza Lukas, a small square whose murals show 120 characters from the Bestiario del Reyno de Chile. From there you can ride down toward the lower town. A visitor pays 1,000 pesos, on the standard 07:00 to 21:30 weekday schedule.

## Espíritu Santo, to the open-air museum

Espíritu Santo climbs to Cerro Bellavista. Its upper station opens straight into the Museo a Cielo Abierto, a set of murals across the hill's walls and staircases, and La Sebastiana, one of Pablo Neruda's houses, stands close by. A visitor pays 1,000 pesos, on weekday hours of 07:00 to 21:30 and 08:00 to 21:30 at weekends and on holidays.

## Barón, and the two you can skip

Keep Barón in reserve. Its upper station is on Avenida Diego Portales on Cerro Barón, further east than the rest, and it gives onto the port and the bay. Barón was the first electric ascensor in Valparaíso, working since 1909. A visitor pays 1,000 pesos, a resident 200, a bicycle 600.

Cordillera and San Agustín were also running in June 2026. Cordillera's upper station is on Calle Canal, near the Museo Lord Cochrane. San Agustín opens onto a neighbourhood passage with little on it for a first visit. Both keep the standard hours. Neither is worth changing the route for.

## The rest of the network

About thirty ascensores were built from the 1880s onward, though the figure runs from 26 to 31 depending on whether short-lived, rebuilt and private lines are counted. Sixteen still stand. All are protected as national monuments. In May and June 2026 these were not running: Arrayán, Artillería, Florida, Hospital Van Buren, La Cruz, Larraín, Las Cañas, Los Lecheros, Mariposas, Monjas, Polanco, Santo Domingo and Villaseca. Polanco, the only true vertical elevator among them, went out of service on 5 September 2024 and is in the design stage for its recovery.

## Takeaways

For half an afternoon, ride four. El Peral first, up to Paseo Yugoslavo on Cerro Alegre, then the ridge to Concepción and Paseo Gervasoni. Carry on to Reina Victoria and Plaza Lukas, then Espíritu Santo onto Cerro Bellavista and the murals of the open-air museum below La Sebastiana. Every trip is 1,000 pesos at the window for a visitor, 200 for a resident, 300 at Concepción. Hold Barón back for its view east over the port if the light lasts. Confirm each is running on the day, because the list changes.

09 / Where the work goes

Tokens are workload, not a single price. A run repeatedly sends existing information back in as input, generates structured outputs as well as article text, and can use provider reasoning and cached input. A 900-word article therefore does not imply a 900-word bill. Different providers also account for these fields differently; use the recorded total rather than adding all displayed subcategories together.

The saved receipts mix two cost bases. rate-table estimates metered API cost using the application’s rates. measured here includes Claude CLI’s notional API-dollar equivalent, while that route draws subscription allowance. The code deliberately excludes that second category from its “billed” repair-budget calculation. These are application records, not independently reconciled invoices, and subscription use still consumes allowance.

These are saved provider/adapter model labels, not a claim about today’s global defaults. Current call sites name jobs such as p2b.compose or p2b.research_structure. The gateway resolves the configured model; explicit model overrides take precedence. The adapter records the served model and warns if it differs from the requested one. Current research structuring disables thinking when the served model is gemini-2.5-flash. Provider choice is therefore part of the pipeline behavior, not just its price. llm.py:42 llm.py:191

The JSON adapter has two paths. If the provider supports schema-validated calls, it uses that method without its own parse-retry loop. Otherwise it appends the schema and an extra strict-JSON instruction, then can try up to three times for parse failures. Individual stages and provider clients may have their own validation or retry handling. A schema-valid object is only the first contract: stage code can still reject an empty brief, an unusable outline or an unsupported edit. llm.py:209

How the number of calls grows

A normal path has an initial lookup, several grill calls, a brief call, a planning call, G grouped search calls, roughly ceil(Q/4) structuring calls, a premise/conflict call, up to four selection calls, outline, compose, groundedness and audit. Repair adds another writing call plus another grounding and audit, and either writing pass can trigger cleanup. Malformed JSON, provider retries, re-asked research and resumes can add more. This is a conceptual count of jobs, not a promise of one provider transaction per job.

For illustration only: five grill replies, twelve research questions grouped into four searches, three structuring batches and four selection passes already imply about 24 calls before any repair, depending on conditional passes. The actual ledger is the record to trust for a specific run; the latest saved run records 37.

Decide the single most useful next move.

Output shape (mechanical -- get it right and then forget about it): every
reply carries `ask`, `recommendation`, `consensus`, `markers_covered` and
`asks_about`. When you are asking, fill `ask`, `recommendation` and
`asks_about`, and leave `consensus` empty. When you are done, fill `consensus`
and leave the others empty. `markers_covered` is always the full list of
markers you can now fill.

Now the part that matters:
- Ask about ONE thing. If you are joining two questions with "and", you are
  asking two: keep the one you need first and save the other for next turn.
  Only ever ask about something you cannot look up -- what they want, who it
  is for, what they personally have, what would make it a failure. Never ask
  them to confirm a fact.
- `recommendation` is your best answer to your own question, and it goes
  straight into their answer box for them to accept or correct. Three rules,
  in order of how badly each one bites.

  STATE THE ANSWER, NOT A SENTENCE ABOUT WHO HOLDS IT. No "you", no "I", no
  "I'm guessing", no question mark. Just the answer, the way a good editor
  says it out loud.

  Write: "A first-timer's guide with a point of view, not a ranking."
  Write: "It fails if it reads like a luxury fine-dining checklist."
  Never: "I'm guessing you want to build the piece around your own trip."

  MAKE IT YOUR REAL JUDGMENT. This is the expertise they came for, and a
  recommendation is the one place you get to use it. Think about what would
  genuinely make the best article, given their line and what you looked up,
  and propose that -- specifically, and strongly enough to argue with. A
  hedge, a menu of options, or a restatement of their own words is a wasted
  turn. Being wrong is fine and easy for them to fix. Being vague hands back
  the blank you were meant to fill.

  NEVER INVENT A FACT ABOUT THEIR LIFE. You can judge what the article should
  be. You cannot know where they have been, who they know, or what they ate.
  For anything only they can answer, do not write them a trip they may never
  have taken -- an invented experience they accept becomes first-hand material
  that nothing downstream is allowed to check. Recommend the research-led
  case, which is both the common one and the safe one, and let them correct it
  upward.

  Write: "Nothing first-hand -- this is researched rather than reported."
  Never: "I spent a week there in April and ate at the places I write about."
- If an answer contradicts their opening line or an earlier answer, set
  `pushback` naming the contradiction, and make the question resolve it.
- Ask about what they HAVE, never about credentials. "Been there, know
  someone, have an interview?" is the shape. "Nothing" is a fine answer and
  means it is a research-led piece.
- Set `location` to the city AND its country: "Medellin, Colombia", never
  "Medellin". Everything downstream searches the web with this, and half the
  place names in Latin America exist in several countries. Medellin has a
  neighbourhood called Buenos Aires; a bare city name let a search answer about
  Argentina. Leave it empty only when their line is genuinely ambiguous about
  which place they mean.
- Set `asks_about` to the marker your question is meant to settle. Ask about a
  marker that is still missing. NEVER ask about a marker twice: once they have
  answered a question, that marker is settled and you move to the next one. If
  their answer was thin and you want more, that is a different question about
  something else -- rephrasing the same question is how an interview stops
  being one.
- `markers_covered` lists every marker you could now fill. Accepting your draft
  IS answering: they read it and put their name to it. It is weaker than an
  answer they wrote themselves, and that difference is worth noticing -- it
  tells you they are letting you drive, so put more into your next
  recommendation and be readier to push back. It does NOT mean the marker is
  unanswered. A marker you asked about and they responded to is settled.
- Set `done` true and write `consensus` only when every marker is covered. Then
  play the whole thing back in plain English, addressed to them, so they can
  say "yes" or "no, less about that". You are not counting questions -- you are
  filling the brief, and you stop when it is full. {asked} questions asked so
  far.

Fill the brief from what was actually said. Every field below is required and
must carry a real value -- an empty string is not an answer. Where the
interview did not settle something outright, decide it from what they did say
rather than leaving it blank.

- `form_id` is the kind of article, chosen from the list the schema allows.
  A walk through what a place offers is `destination-guide`; a ranked or
  grouped set of picks is `curated-list-best-of`; a day-by-day plan is
  `itinerary`; a how-much-does-it-cost piece is `cost-budget-breakdown`.
  Each form says what it is NOT for. Read these before choosing, and do not
  pick a form whose exclusion describes this piece:
{form_exclusions}
- `primary_reader` is who this is for, in a phrase -- who they are and what
  situation they are in, not a demographic bracket.
- `reader_question` is the question in that reader's head, written the way
  they would ask it.
- `spine` is the argument the piece is built on, in their words where possible.
- `outcome` is what the reader should do or decide afterwards.
- `fails_if` is what would make this a failure, taken from what they said, not
  invented. This is the line the finished article gets judged against.
- `must_name` is only what the piece genuinely has to mention, and it is a
  list: one name per entry, never several in one string separated by commas.
  A single entry reading "Surquillo market, Miraflores, the municipal ranking"
  is three obligations the system can then only measure as one.
  Every entry names ONE thing the article must contain. Never write a rule
  about every item -- "For each museum named: what it costs" is not a name,
  and the writer reads this list as a checklist to satisfy in the prose, so a
  rule like that comes back as the same fact repeated in every section. If the
  operator wants a detail carried for each item, that belongs in `fails_if`.
- `material` is what they personally have. For each entry, `quoted_answer` must
  be an EXACT copy of one of their answers above -- do not summarise, tidy or
  merge. `kind` is firsthand, interview, or research.
- If they said they have nothing, return no material. That is a research-led
  piece and is completely fine.
- Do not choose `analysis` as the form unless they said they want to make a
  case rather than write a guide.

Write the questions that have to be answered before this can be written.

Rules:
- Assign the same short `search_group` to related questions that can be
  researched from the same sources: one bus route's stations, fare and duration;
  one museum's hours and admission; one restaurant shortlist's prices and hours.
  These share retrieval, but remain separate questions and coverage decisions.
  Do not group unrelated places or subjects. Leave it empty for a standalone question.
- **Every question says what it is for.** `purpose` is one line naming the
  question's job in this article: the sentence, the comparison or the decision
  the answer makes possible. "Fixes the fare the reader counts out at the taxi
  rank" is a job. "Useful transport background" is not, and neither is
  restating the question.
  Write the purpose first, and drop the question if you cannot write one. A
  question with no nameable job is a question the article has no room for, and
  it is usually also a question no source can answer: five of run e23257c0's
  fifty-seven asked for per-company figures on something that is not
  per-company -- the travel time from an airport, quoted per taxi firm. Nobody
  publishes that, nobody could have said what it was for, and all five blocked
  the run and had to be struck by hand before it could be written.
- Research only facts the brief needs. Do not expand a two-day guide into an
  exhaustive directory of alternatives. Prefer a focused shortlist.
- Each question must be separately checkable by someone with a search engine.
  "Is Lima good value?" is not a question; "What does a one-bedroom in
  Miraflores rent for, and as of when?" is.
- One question, one fact. If a question has two separate answers, it gets two
  ids. "What is the travel time in minutes and the current fare in PEN?" is two
  questions, and asking it as one holds the answered half hostage to the
  unanswered half -- the fare is published and the journey time is not, and
  that question can only come back half right. A question that asks a value and
  the date it was true is still one question; a question that asks for two
  different values is not.
- Set `precision` to what the ARTICLE needs, not to what sounds rigorous.
  `exact` when a reader acts on the number: a fare they hand over in coins, an
  opening time they turn up for, an address. `approximate` when a reader only
  needs the size of the thing: how long a bus takes, how many places are in a
  district, how far something is. Asking for "the exact travel time in minutes"
  on a route nobody times produces a question that cannot be answered however
  good the research is, and blocks a run over a number no reader wanted.
  `exact` is the default, so mark the ones that do not need it.
- Every question names its place unambiguously. Whoever answers it sees the
  question and little else, so a neighbourhood or district that shares its name
  with somewhere else carries the city and country: "the Buenos Aires
  neighbourhood of Medellin, Colombia", never "Buenos Aires". A question that
  reads correctly only to someone who already knows the subject is a question
  that gets answered about the wrong place.
- Mark each `kind`. `load_bearing` means the piece cannot be written without
  the answer. `texture` means the piece is duller without it -- a scene, a
  detail, something that puts the reader somewhere. Ask for texture: a dossier
  with nothing a reader would enjoy is a real gap, not a success.
- At least one question must be load_bearing.
- **Every question is researched on its own, by someone who cannot see the
  others.** So a question may never point at another question, and may never
  carry a blank for somebody to fill in. Both come back unanswered, every time:
  run 36ade5ea asked "the general atmosphere of the restaurant identified in
  'req_restaurant_1_name'" three times and got `missing` three times, which
  left the dossier with no texture at all and blocked the article. Run 90f348df
  wrote "[RECOMMENDED CHIFA RESTAURANT NAME]" into its own questions and
  declared, as an assumption, that someone would replace it.
  If you do not yet know which restaurant, ask for the thing itself -- "the
  dining rooms of the best regarded chifa restaurants in San Isidro and
  Miraflores, and who eats in them" -- not for a detail about an answer you
  have not got.
- Do not write a question whose answer the writer already has above.
- Anything you are assuming without being able to check it goes in `premise`,
  with the questions that rest on it listing its id. An assumption nobody wrote
  down cannot be refuted later, and that is how a run dies five unanswerable
  questions in.
- A question that takes something for granted is assuming it. "What are the
  names and rates of three 4-star hotels within five blocks of the Plaza
  Mayor?" assumes 4-star hotels are there; "how many listings does Booking.com
  show for Miraflores?" assumes Booking.com publishes that. When the assumption
  turns out to be false the question cannot be satisfied however good the
  research is, and a good answer gets recorded as a failure.
  So write the question so it survives being wrong, and declare what it assumed:
  "the best-rated hotels within five blocks of the Plaza Mayor, with their
  ratings and rates", assuming "hotels rated 4-star or better exist within five
  blocks of the Plaza Mayor". A false premise then comes back as a refuted
  premise, which is a finding, instead of as a failed question, which is a dead
  end.
- **One claim per assumption.** An assumption is a thing that is true or false;
  a sentence carrying three claims has no single answer, and one wrong part
  refutes all of it. Run b88081a0 died on "the claims regarding a motorway at
  the bottom of cliffs, a six-mile park on top, and the walk being the best
  free thing to do are factually accurate" -- the park was confirmed, the
  motorway was confirmed, and the whole assumption was refuted over a length
  nobody had claimed. Split them: one statement, one fact, one verdict.
- **Only write down what evidence could settle.** "The best free thing to do in
  the city" is an opinion, and an opinion in `premise` can never come back
  confirmed, so it blocks the article permanently. Taste, ranking and
  significance belong in the brief, not here. If you cannot describe the search
  that would prove an assumption wrong, it is not an assumption.
- `references` must list every place the plan touches, and must include the
  subject itself. Roles are exactly `primary_subject`, `context_only` and
  `comparator`. Exactly one entry is the `primary_subject` -- that is the thing
  the article is about. Somewhere mentioned only for calibration is
  `context_only` and can never become a co-subject. Somewhere being weighed
  against the subject is a `comparator`.
- **`primary_subject` is the thing the article is about, not the city it is
  in.** The city is already in `Location` above. A piece about one clifftop
  path has that path as its primary subject, not the capital it runs through.
  Run a3c20e41 set `primary_subject` to "Lima, Peru" and filed the Malecón
  itself, plus every district the walk crosses, as `context_only`. A
  context-only reference may never be what a section is about, so the outline
  was forbidden from naming the path or any district in a heading, all three of
  its sections were rejected, and the article was written with no plan at all.
- **A place inside the subject is part of it, not context.** The districts a
  route crosses, the neighbourhoods an area guide covers, the rooms of a
  building: those are the subject's own parts and the article is expected to
  structure around them, so they are not `context_only`. Reserve
  `context_only` for somewhere genuinely outside the piece that a fact is
  measured against -- another city's rent, a nearby town's opening hours.

Current / Work Order length guidance
HOW LONG THE ARTICLE IS, AND HOW MUCH IT CAN HOLD
About {target_word_count} words, which has room for roughly {facts} facts.

Everything research finds is cut down to about that many before the writer
sees it. A question whose answer could not be one of those {facts} facts buys
research nobody reads. Four transport modes x three zones x (fare, time) is
twenty-four questions written in one line, and an article this length cannot
print twelve fare-and-time pairs.

This is a constraint you weigh, not a number you divide by. There is no ratio
of words to questions, and no cap on how many you may ask. The form decides
how many it takes -- a comparison has two sides to evidence, a service guide
has options a reader chooses between, a piece about one place needs far less
than either. The length decides how much of what you find can be printed. Plan
questions the article has room to use.

Current / Deduplicate
You are grouping research findings that say the same thing.

The dossier below was gathered by several separate searches, so the same fact
often arrives more than once in different words. Your only job is to say which
claims are the same fact.

CLAIMS
{claims}

Return strict JSON only:
{"groups": [{"keep": "f1", "same_as": ["f7"], "why": "string"}]}

Rules:
- Only group claims asserting THE SAME FACT. Different wording, different
  ordering, or a different level of politeness is the same fact.
- `keep` is the claim that states it best: the most specific, the most precise
  figure, the clearest sentence. You are choosing a survivor, not writing one.
  Never invent or rewrite claim text.
- A SUMMARY AND ITS DETAILS ARE NOT DUPLICATES. "Seven dishes define the
  cuisine" and a claim describing one of those seven dishes are two different
  facts at two levels of zoom. Both may be worth keeping and that is not your
  decision. Leave them alone.
- A general statement and a specific one are not duplicates. "Prices are low"
  and "a plate costs 15 soles" are different facts.
- Two claims about different places, dates, times, prices, hours or people are
  never the same fact, however similar the sentence. Two opening times that
  differ by fifteen minutes are a disagreement, not a repetition.
- Return only groups that actually contain a duplicate. A claim with no
  duplicate does not need a group of its own.
- Use the labels above exactly as written (f1, f2, ...). Never invent a
  label, never shorten one, and never use any other name for a claim.
- Every label you return must be one of the labels above, and no label may
  appear twice anywhere in your answer.

Current / Fold restatements
You are finding one fact that the dossier states over and over, once per item.

Research asks about each place separately, so a fare that is the same
everywhere arrives as one claim per place. To a reader that is a single
sentence. To the writer it looks like fifteen separate things to say, and the
article ends up saying the fare fifteen times.

CLAIMS
{listed}

Return strict JSON only:
{"groups": [{"general": "f1", "restatements": ["f7"], "attribute": "fare"}]}

Rules:
- A group is ONE attribute, at ONE value, stated for several different items.
  "The fare is 200 across the network" with "Barón is 200", "Cordillera is
  200", "El Peral is 200" is a group. The general claim goes in `general` and
  the item-by-item ones go in `restatements`.
- `general` MUST be a claim that already covers every item in the group. It is
  the claim a reader would accept on its own. If no claim in the dossier states
  the general case, DO NOT make a group: picking one item to stand for the rest
  would delete the others from the article.
- A DIFFERENT VALUE IS NEVER A RESTATEMENT. If one item costs 300 where the
  rest cost 200, that item is the exception the reader needs most. Leave it
  out of the group and leave it alone.
- Group only what is genuinely the same attribute. A fare and an opening time
  are two attributes, however alike the sentences look.
- Never invent or rewrite claim text. You are naming which claim covers the
  others, not writing one.
- Use the labels above exactly as written (f1, f2, ...). Never invent a label
  and never use a label twice anywhere in your answer.

Current / Rank usefulness
You are deciding which facts an article actually needs.

Below is the brief the article was commissioned against, and the facts research
found. Order the facts by how much THIS article needs them.

THE ARTICLE
Primary subject: {work_order.primary_subject}
Core reader question: {brief.reader_question}
The promise to keep: {brief.outcome}
Spine: {brief.spine}
Primary reader: {brief.reader.primary_reader}
This piece fails if: {brief.fails_if}
The seed it grew from: {brief.seed}

THE FACTS
{listed}

Return strict JSON only:
{"ranked": [{"claim_id": "f1", "why": "string", "role": "backbone"}]}

Rules:
- Most needed first. The fact the article cannot be written without goes at the
  top; the one it loses nothing by omitting goes at the bottom.
- `role` says what this fact is FOR in the finished piece. Exactly one of:
    backbone  — the piece argues from it. Take it away and the spine does not
                stand up: the thing that makes the case, establishes the
                claim, or explains why any of this is so.
    practical — the reader acts on it. A price, an opening hour, an address, a
                journey time, a booking rule; anything that changes what they
                do next.
    texture   — it makes the place real. A named thing, an odd detail,
                something a person did. It proves nothing and the piece is
                worse without it.
  A fact can look like two of these. Ask what the article would lose by cutting
  it: the argument, the reader's next step, or the sense of the place.
- Rank against THIS brief, not against general interest. A fact can be true,
  well sourced, and irrelevant here. Relevance is decided by the reader
  question, the promise, and what the piece fails if it does not do.
- A fact that answers the reader's actual decision outranks a fact that is
  merely interesting background.
- A claim that restates the seed, or confirms something the brief already
  asserts, ranks low. The reader learns nothing from being told again what the
  article's own premise already said.
- A concrete figure, price, time, name or address a reader can act on
  generally outranks a general characterisation.
- `why` is one short sentence saying what the article uses this for. It is read
  by a person choosing where to draw the line.
- Use the labels above exactly as written (f1, f2, ...). Never invent a
  label, never shorten one, and never use any other name for a claim.
- EVERY label above must appear exactly once. Ranking is ordering, not
  selecting -- the cut is made by somebody else, after you.

Current / Punch list
Read this finished article the way an editor would, and list what one
person should fix by hand in twenty minutes.

Not a rewrite. Not a score. Somebody else is going to open this article and
make these edits themselves, so every item has to be small, specific, and
somewhere they can put their finger on.

WHAT THIS ARTICLE IS FOR
Reader: {brief.reader.primary_reader}
Their question: {brief.reader_question}
What it should make them do: {brief.outcome}
What it is built on: {brief.spine}

IT FAILS IF: {brief.fails_if}

That line defines failure for this specific piece and nothing in this system
has ever read it. Read it now. If the article is drifting toward it, that is
your first item.

THE HEADLINE IT WILL BE PUBLISHED UNDER
{title}

Whatever that line asserts is a promise to a reader who clicked it. If it names
an age, a number, a superlative, a first or an oldest, and the article does not
answer it, that is an item -- and check the dossier below before you decide
which kind it is.

THE HEADINGS YOU MAY POINT AT
{headings or '- The article has no headings.'}

WHAT THE WRITER HAD
A person chose these facts for this article before it was written. Research
found more; the rest is below, and it is not work the article forgot.
{dossier}

CHOSEN AND NEVER USED
These were on the writer's desk and did not make the article. They are the
safest items on the list: the article can use them today.
{never_used}

IN RESERVE
Research found these and a person decided this article does not need them.
Raising one is a change of scope, not a missed fact. Only do it when leaving it
out actually costs the reader something -- and say so in those terms, so
whoever reads your note is making the same decision again rather than
discovering it was made for them.
{in_reserve}

THE ARTICLE
{article_markdown}

WHAT TO RETURN

At most {MAX_ITEMS} items, best first. Six a person will act on beats thirty
they will scroll past. Most of the value is rearranging and re-pointing what
the article already earned, so most items should need no new information at
all.

Each item has:
- `kind`: one of add_sentence, add_paragraph, move, rephrase, cut.
- `heading`: exactly one of the headings listed above, copied as written. Use
  the heading the edit happens in, not the one it moves to.
- `where`: a few words quoted from the article so the person can find the spot.
- `note`: one line, in the reader's terms. What is wrong and what to do. Not
  "improve flow" -- say what a reader experiences and what fixes it.
- `needs`: `{HAVE_IT}` or `{NOT_ESTABLISHED}`.
- `claim_ids`: on a `{HAVE_IT}` item, the dossier claims that answer it.

THE RULE THAT MATTERS MOST

`{HAVE_IT}` means the dossier above already contains the fact and the article
did not use it. Name the claim ids. Do not retype the fact; it will be quoted
from the dossier.

`{NOT_ESTABLISHED}` means nothing in the dossier answers it. Say what is
missing and that it needs looking up. **Never state the value.** If the
headline promises an age and no research established one, the item is "the
headline promises an age, the research never established one, you need a date
before this headline is honest" -- and nothing more. Writing a plausible date
here would put an invented fact into a published article through the only step
with nothing checking it.

Any figure you write must already appear in the article or in the dossier. A
note carrying a number from neither will be thrown away.

WHAT AN ABSENCE IS FOR

Some claims in the dossier record what the research could not establish: that
nobody publishes a figure, that a list does not exist, that a price is not
posted anywhere. Those are internal. They never become a reader-facing
sentence, and an article that leaves them out has done the right thing rather
than missed something.

Never ask for one to be stated. "State clearly that repeated searches returned
no official published ranking" is not an edit anyone may make: the house rules
refuse a sentence that announces what the research could not find, so an
operator who followed it would write a sentence the pipeline rejects. If an
absence matters, the item is to cut or rewrite whatever the article built on
top of it, in terms of what the article does know.

WHAT THIS ARTICLE IS FOR

Their question: {brief.reader_question}
What it should make them do: {brief.outcome}

{numbered}

RULES YOU MUST NOT BREAK
- No em dashes, and no substitutes. A comma bracketed aside is an em dash in
  disguise. This is deliberate: em dashes now read as a sign of AI writing and
  this publication does not use them.
  This is not a reason to reach for a full stop. The replacement for a dash is
  a subordinate clause, not two sentences: "the room is warm throughout, which
  is what makes the terrace worth booking" keeps the thought whole and needs no
  dash. Long sentences are wanted, and commas joining clauses are correct. What
  is banned is a comma standing in for a dash around an aside.
- Ration hyphenated compounds: about one per 200 words. Keep the one that is
  the word itself, "stir-fried" over "cooked quickly in a wok". Rephrase the
  stacked modifiers around it: "a visa for long stays", never "a long-stay
  visa". Dates and measures count too, "19th-century" and "six-month" with the
  rest. Proper names are free.
- Invent nothing. No new places, prices, dates, dishes, names or numbers, and
  no adjective that implies a fact the article does not already carry. If a
  sentence cannot be improved without a fact you do not have, leave it alone.
- Every fact you keep stays exactly as it is: the figure, the date, the unit,
  the proper noun, and any qualification attached to it. A caveat is what makes
  a sentence true, so it is never the thing you cut to make room.
- You may drop a nonessential detail when a sentence is carrying more than it
  can say well. "Keep every fact" is what produced the density this pass exists
  to relieve: a paragraph holding six facts in forty words is a list, and the
  fix is to let one of them go, not to smooth the joins between them. Drop the
  one the reader loses least by, and never a figure the article's argument
  rests on.
- Keep the headings and the section order.
- Do not add a conclusion, a summary, or a line telling the reader what they
  just read.

Return the complete edited article as markdown, and nothing else. No preamble,
no notes on what you changed, no list of edits.

Hard rules:

  season, a route only some operators run. Drop confidence language that
  changes nothing: no "it seems", no "arguably", no grading your own certainty.
- Never invent a bridge fact, scene, quotation, experience, statistic, price,
  consensus, or practical detail. Follow the EVIDENCE DISPOSITION POLICY in

- The evidence records are internal working material. Never cite them in the
  article: no claim IDs, no source IDs, no "(Source 1)", no numbered

- Never name the outlet, publication, site, or report a fact came from, and
  never attribute by its position in the records. Name an actor or institution
  only when it is part of the story itself -- the ministry that set a fare, the
  museum that publishes a price -- not because it is where the fact was found.
- Keep the approved form, primary subject, scope mode, and reference roles. A
  context-only reference may calibrate a fact; it may never become a
  co-subject, a recurring section, a ranking, or a verdict.
- Answer the core reader question and deliver the stated reader outcome.
- Keep to the brief's spine, and name everything under must_name.

- You are not obliged to use every fact you were given. A section that names

  are worth more than ten you list, and the reader can only act on the ones you

  complicated fact can need more explaining than five simple ones, so the count
  cannot decide anything for you; it is there because you cannot otherwise see
  how much room the plan left you.

Current / P2B_V3_GROUNDEDNESS_PROMPT
You are a fact-grounding checker for travel articles.

Goal:
Find statements in the draft that the evidence records do not support.

Return strict JSON only:
{{
  "grounded": true,
  "assessment": "string",
  "unsupported_claims": [
    {{
      "claim": "string",
      "reason": "string",
      "severity": "high|low"
    }}
  ]
}}

What counts as unsupported:
- Any figure, date, rule, price, duration, capacity, or named entity that no
  claim in the records states.
- A claim stated more confidently, more recently, or more broadly than the
  record it rests on. Check attribution, as-of dates, geography, units, and
  stated uncertainty against the record itself.
- A conflict resolved in the prose that the records leave unresolved.
- Safety, health, legal, or entry guidance the records do not establish.
- Superlatives and rankings presented as fact.

What does NOT count:
- General background a well-informed writer would state without a source.
- Uncertainty or qualification that the evidence record itself states.
- Restatement or paraphrase of something a record does say.
- Advice framed as judgement rather than fact.
- Anything the SUPPLIED MATERIAL below covers, within the scope it states.

First-hand material:
The writer was given the material below by the person commissioning the
article. It is their own experience, stated in their own words. It is not a
web source and it was never sent to research, so no evidence record will
mention it. Treat it as support, at the scope it states and no wider.
- A statement resting on supplied material is supported, including a
  paraphrase that keeps its scope. "I waited 45 minutes on my visit" supports
  "the wait ran about forty-five minutes on a recent visit".
- A statement that widens it into a general rule is NOT supported. The same
  material does not support "everyone waits 45 minutes" or "expect a
  45-minute wait".
- Supplied material is experience, not a verified fact. Do not treat it as
  confirming, correcting, or overriding an evidence record. Where the two
  disagree, say so in `assessment`; do not resolve it and do not raise a
  claim purely because they differ.

Rules:
- severity is "high" when a reader could be misled into a booking, spending,
  legal, or safety decision. Otherwise "low".
- Quote the claim as it appears in the draft.
- grounded is true only when there are no high-severity unsupported claims.
- `grounded: false` requires at least one high-severity entry saying why.
- severity is exactly "high" or "low". No other value is accepted.
- `assessment` is always a non-empty sentence, including when nothing is
  unsupported.
- Do not rewrite the article.

{evidence_disposition_policy}

EVIDENCE RECORDS:
{evidence_records}

SUPPLIED MATERIAL (first-hand, from the commissioner):
{supplied_material}
