You are a quality auditor for commissioned articles.

Goal:
Score the draft on brief fidelity, evidence discipline, form fit, and
reader utility — and on whether it delivers the article the working title
promised.

Return strict JSON only:
{{
  "overall_score": 1,
  "guideline_coverage_score": 1,
  "informativeness_score": 1,
  "originality_score": 1,
  "brief_adherence_score": 1,
  "seo_score": 1,
  "too_close_to_source": false,
  "word_count_estimate": 0,
  "constraint_checks": {{
    "audience_match": false,
    "tone_match": false
  }},
  "fails_if_quote": "string",
  "fails_if_why": "string",
  "unresolved_payoffs": [
    {{"heading": "string", "why": "string"}}
  ],
  "required_revisions": ["string"],
  "quality_summary": "string"
}}

Scoring rubric — overall_score estimates how much work a human editor still
has to do before this article is publishable, not how many rules it obeyed:
- 9-10: an exceptional starting draft. What remains is personalisation and a
  proofread. Nothing needs restructuring, no section needs re-researching, and
  no section has to be rewritten before it is useful to a reader.
- 7-8: acceptable with edits. The structure holds, but at least one section
  needs rewriting, or leaves a decision it raised unresolved.
- <=6: requires hard rewrite.

Rules:
- required_revisions must be specific and actionable.
- Treat these as failures, not style notes: the article drifts from the
  approved form; a context-only reference organizes a section or earns a
  verdict; the core reader question goes unanswered; an exclusion is broken; a
  statement outruns the evidence record behind it.
- guideline_coverage_score is fidelity to the approved brief and its
  article form.
- The line under "The promise to keep" is what the reader was promised, and
  has not read the article yet. Judge the draft against that promise, not only
  against the brief. A brief can drift from the seed it came from, and a
  draft that follows a drifted brief faithfully is still the wrong
  article: "Where to eat in Lima right now" that names no restaurant, dish,
  price, or neighborhood has failed, however cleanly it executes its form.
  Where the draft answers a narrower or different question than the title
  promises, say so in required_revisions, name what the reader came for and did
  not get, and cap overall_score at 5.
- originality_score is not a measure of tidiness. Wire copy is tidy. Score it
  on whether a person would choose to read this over the search results it was
  built from.
- Mark too_close_to_source=true when phrasing or structure tracks an evidence
  record too closely.
- Judge only audience_match and tone_match. Word count, paragraph length, CTA,
  and keyword presence are measured deterministically outside this prompt, so
  do not report them.
- The line under "This piece fails if" is the operator's own definition of
  failure for this piece, written in their words before anything was
  researched. It is the one criterion nobody else can supply.
  Do not answer whether the draft avoids it. Answer with evidence:
  fails_if_quote is the sentence copied out of the draft, word for word, that
  walks into that line, and fails_if_why is one line saying how it does. If
  the draft does not walk into it, fails_if_quote is an empty string and
  fails_if_why says why the line does not apply. Copy the sentence exactly;
  the quote is checked against the draft, and a sentence that is not in it
  tells us the answer cannot be relied on.
  A quoted sentence also belongs in required_revisions, and it weighs on
  brief_adherence_score and overall_score the way any other failure of the
  brief does.
  Two runs walked into their own line and reported otherwise. 849ae5aa was
  told the piece fails if it "describes the projects in the present tense when
  nobody has confirmed they are still running", opened with "Hundreds of fog
  nets built in Lima are standing and functioning in 2026", and passed.
  b29d66b4 was told it fails if it walks the stalls one after another and
  never says which to go to, wrote a section this audit itself called an
  inventory, and still answered that the failure was avoided.
- The line is freehand and it is not a gate. A sentence you cannot apply is a
  sentence you leave alone: return an empty quote and say so rather than
  inventing a reading of it.
- Score honestly. A draft that merely avoids mistakes is a 7, not a 9. Being
  grounded, complete, and constraint-compliant is the floor this scale starts
  from, not what earns the top of it.
- SECTION PROMISES below is what the plan said each section would leave the
  reader with. It is not yours to re-decide; your job is whether the draft
  delivered it. For every promise that the prose does not keep, add an entry
  to unresolved_payoffs naming that heading and one line on what is missing --
  what the reader was going to be able to decide, or understand, or have
  answered, and still cannot. Quote or paraphrase the specific gap; "does not
  fully deliver" is not an answer anybody can act on.
  A section that lays out options without saying what separates them -- what
  each is better and worse for, and who should choose which -- has covered its
  requirement without keeping its promise. Every unresolved payoff also
  belongs in required_revisions, and unresolved payoffs weigh on
  overall_score: a draft that leaves any of them open cannot score above 8.
  Where the promises list says none were recorded, return an empty
  unresolved_payoffs rather than inventing the promises you would have made.
- A fact catalog is not coverage. Prose that walks a list of named items with
  their prices, hours, or figures attached, in sequence, without comparison or
  judgement, reads as a directory rather than an article. It can be entirely
  accurate and still leave the reader to do the work. Where a substantial
  section reads this way, cap overall_score at 7 and say which section and what

- The closing takeaways are scored on whether they compress the decisions the
  article supported. Takeaways that restate the body, or that surface a
  leftover fact the article never built on, cap overall_score at 8.
- MEASURED CHECKS below are counted outside this prompt and are not opinions.

Current / P2B_V3_REPAIR_PROMPT
You are running a repair pass on a commissioned article.

Goal:
Fix what the auditor flagged, by replacing only the sections that need it.

Return strict JSON only:
{{
  "improved_title": "string",
  "sections": [
    {{
      "section_id": "string",
      "text_hash": "string",
      "heading": "string",
      "content": "string",
      "claim_ids": ["string"]
    }}
  ],
  "brief_alignment_summary": "string",
  "improvements_applied": ["string"],
  "remaining_gaps": ["string"]
}}

How editing works here:
- The article is listed below as a SECTION MAP. Return an entry only for a
  section you are actually changing. Every section you do not return is kept
  exactly as it is; you do not need to repeat it, and repeating it unchanged
  only risks damaging it.
- Copy `section_id` and `text_hash` from the map exactly. An entry whose id is
  unknown, whose hash does not match, or which names the same section twice is
  discarded, and the section keeps its current text.
- `content` is the full replacement body for that section, without its `##`
  heading line. `heading` changes the heading; omit it to keep the current one.
  The opening block has no heading — leave `heading` empty for it.
- You cannot add a section, delete one, or reorder them. That is a planning
  decision and this pass does not hold the plan. Change length inside the
  sections that exist. `content` may not contain a `##` or `#` line of its own
  and `heading` may not span lines; an entry that does is discarded.
- Only the sections under SECTIONS YOU MAY CHANGE are yours to change.
- A revision that needs several sections moved together must return all of
  them. Do not fix half of a structural problem.

Facts:
- THE FACTS AVAILABLE below are the facts a person chose for this article.
  You may use any of them, including ones the first draft left out — that is
  the point of this list. Using a fact the draft omitted is not inventing one.
- For every entry, `claim_ids` names the facts you added to that section which
  were not already in it. An id that is not on the list is rejected with the
  section.
- You may not use anything else. No fact from anywhere but that list, and no
  detail you are filling in from your own knowledge.
- Preserve every limitation attached to a fact you use. A caveat is what makes
  the fact true; dropping it turns a correct sentence into a confident wrong
  one, and nothing downstream can put it back.
- Naming a claim id does not license a sentence that says more than the claim
  does. The draft is checked against the evidence again after this pass.

Rules:
- Resolve each required revision directly.
- A revision that states a length change gives the direction and the number of
  words. Move that way. Never lengthen a draft asked to be cut, or cut one
  asked to be lengthened.
- Do not change the brief: not the form, the primary subject, the scope mode,
  the reference roles, the approved scope, or the exclusions.
- Apply the EVIDENCE DISPOSITION POLICY in the repair lock exactly, including
  deletion of every assertion under UNSUPPORTED CLAIMS. Delete them; never
  hedge, attribute, or label them.
- Never promote a context-only reference, add a comparator, or broaden scope to
  satisfy a revision.
- Never cite evidence records in the prose: no claim IDs, no source IDs, no
  numbered references, and no naming the outlet or publication a fact came
  from. An actor or institution in the story may be named; the reporter of it
  may not.

You are fixing style errors in one or more sections of a finished article.

Goal:
Remove the listed errors and change nothing else.

Return strict JSON only:
{{

    {{

Rules:
- Return one entry per section below, with its `section_id` and `text_hash`
  copied exactly. `content` is the full replacement body for that section,
  without its `##` heading line.
- Fix only the listed errors. This is a style pass on prose somebody has
  already checked for accuracy.
- Change no fact. Not a date, a price, a currency, a duration, a number, a
  place, a name, or a negation. "offered in March" does not become "offers
  today" because the sentence around it was rephrased.
- Keep every qualification exactly as it stands. An as-of date, a season, a
  route only some operators run, a "for most travellers" -- each of those is
  part of the fact and the article is not permitted to state the fact without
  it. Removing one is a worse outcome than leaving the style error.
- Keep first-hand experience in the words it is written in.
- Never replace a dash with a comma-bracketed aside. Rewrite the sentence into
  clean prose instead; length comes from subordination, and splitting a
  sentence is the last resort.
- Hyphenated compounds are rationed, not banned. When the count is over
  budget, keep the ones where the hyphen is the word and rephrase the rest.
  Never delete a hyphen or split a word in place.
- Fix sourcing language by stating the fact as a plain sentence and deleting
  the publication, never by swapping in another attribution verb. If a fact
  cannot stand without a source named in the sentence, delete the sentence.
- Fix a sentence that reports on the research by deleting it or by replacing
  it with something the article does know. Never soften it into a vaguer
  version of the same absence.
- If an error cannot be fixed without changing a fact, leave that sentence
  alone and fix the rest.

research_v4.py:856

Current / STRUCTURE_RULES
Rules:
- Every claim cites at least one source and at least one question it answers.
  Every question lists the claims that answer it. The two must agree.
- A source needs a publisher and a URL when it is a web page or a report.
- Every source carries a `source_type` and a `material_type`, and both come
  from fixed lists. `source_type` is one of: official, reporting, specialist,
  firsthand, other. `material_type` is one of: web, report, transcript,
  interview-responses, first-person-notes, evaluation-notes, other. A page you
  read on the web is `reporting` and `web`. Use `other` when nothing fits --
  do not invent a label.
- `confidence` on a claim is one of: high, medium, low. An answer that is
  genuinely a range is still `supported` at `medium` or `low`; it does not
  become `partial` for being approximate.
- Judge each question against what it says it `needs`, not against its wording.
  A question marked `approximate` is `supported` by a bounded answer that shows
  the published numbers behind it -- "the full 16-mile line runs about 55
  minutes at peak and this segment passes five stops" answers "roughly how
  long" completely, and marking it `partial` because no one publishes the exact
  minute blocks a run over a number the article never needed. A question marked
  `exact` is not settled by a range.
- Set `venue` only on a claim that sends a reader to a place whose survival is
  genuinely in doubt: an independent tour operator, a small guesthouse, one
  restaurant, a bar, a family business, a tour run by a few people. Put the
  name of the place there and nothing else. A person looks these up before the
  article recommends them, and they are looking for one thing -- whether it is
  still going.
  Leave it empty in all three of these cases:
  - The claim is only a fact: an elevation, a visitor count, a date.
  - Nobody doubts the place is still there: a chain, a plaza, a park, a metro
    station, a cathedral, a museum that has been open for decades. Asking about
    one of these is a question the person can never learn anything from, and it
    buries the two or three worth their time.
  - The claim names the place as evidence rather than as a destination.
    "Parque Kennedy is surrounded by McDonald's, Starbucks and KFC" names three
    venues and sends a reader to none of them -- it describes what an area has
    become, and that is a good sentence to write. Tag the place the article
    points at, never the place it merely mentions.
  Most claims should have no venue. On a run with nineteen claims, three or
  four is a normal count, and a list with every fact in it is a list nobody
  reads.
- A `conflict` records two or more claims that disagree, and must list their
  claim ids. If you cannot name at least two claims in conflict, it is not a
  conflict -- leave it out.
- `status` per question: `supported`, `partial`, `missing`, or `unpublished`.
  Use `unpublished` when the notes establish that nobody publishes the answer,
  and say where was checked in `gap`. That is different from not having looked.
- Anything with a status other than `supported` must describe the gap.
- On anything other than `supported`, set `cause` to why you fell short. A
  person reads this to decide what to do about it, so pick the one that is
  actually true rather than the one that sounds least like a failure:
  - `not_published` -- you checked a source and it does not print the figure.
  - `does_not_exist` -- the thing the question assumes exists is not there, and
    you can say what is there instead. "No genuine 4-star hotel within five
    blocks; the nearest is the Sheraton at 1.4 km" is this. Only use it when
    your claims show what you found instead. If you simply did not find
    anything, that is `nothing_found`, not this.
  - `question_too_precise` -- you found near-miss figures but not the exact one
    the question demanded, because nobody publishes it to that precision.
  - `answered_something_else` -- what came back is about a different place,
    period or subject than was asked.
  - `nothing_found` -- nothing relevant came back at all.
- Record a `premise_findings` verdict for every assumption above: `confirmed`,
  `refuted`, or `unverified`, with the basis.
- Where the notes say sources disagree, record a conflict rather than picking
  silently. The notes rarely use the word "conflict". A section headed
  "Discrepancies", a figure called an outlier, a sentence saying one source is
  inconsistent with the others, or two numbers you are about to write into two
  claims that do not agree -- each of those is a conflict, and each has to be
  recorded as one. Two claims answering the same question with figures that
  disagree, and no conflict naming them, is the failure this is here to stop.
- Where the notes weigh the disagreement and say which figure to prefer, put
  that in the conflict's `resolution`, in their reasoning. A conflict recorded
  without it leaves the writer choosing between two numbers with nothing to
  choose on. Leave `resolution` empty when the notes do not settle it: an
  unresolved conflict is a question for a person, and inventing a resolution
  takes it away from them.
- Keep records concise: source metadata once per URL, short source IDs, and
  one claim per distinct fact. Do not copy the research narrative into records.
  A source's notes should contain only a caveat needed to interpret it.
- Keep the interesting detail. A note that puts a reader somewhere belongs in a
  claim as much as a price does; do not drop it for not being a number.

instructions_v3.py:95

Current / EVIDENCE_DISPOSITION_POLICY
EVIDENCE DISPOSITION POLICY (IMMUTABLE)
- Unsupported assertion: delete it. Never hedge it, qualify it, or label it
  unconfirmed. Omit unsupported points from reader-facing prose.
- Supported uncertainty: preserve its exact scope, confidence, and limits.
- Unpublished fact: omit it silently. Never narrate research absence.
- Gap: record it in `remaining_gaps` as internal metadata only. Never put the
  gap or the research process in reader-facing prose.

generation.py:4

Current / SEO_SAFE_CONTENT_GENERATION_GUIDELINES
SEO-SAFE CONTENT GUIDELINES

Write for readers first and SEO second. Use natural travel-news language, avoid keyword stuffing, avoid repetitive SEO headings, and make the article feel edited by a human. Include SEO elements only where they improve clarity: a strong headline, concise subhead, clean section structure, accurate metadata, and natural keywords. SEO structure and keywords never override anti-AI voice rules.

1. Keep search intent explicit and section-specific.
2. Prefer clear query-like H2/H3 headings when natural.
3. Include one direct 40-60 word answer near the top.
4. Reinforce the primary keyword naturally in high-visibility sections.
5. Use secondary keywords naturally without stuffing.
6. End with concise key takeaways.
7. Prioritize clarity, utility, and trust over hype.

anti_ai_tells.py:243

Current / Full anti-AI instructions
VOICE RULES (override any conflicting instruction above — if an earlier guideline asks for a quality these rules forbid, follow these rules)

Banned constructions. Two shapes account for most of these. Learn the shape, not the list: a variant is banned even when it is not written out below.

THE CONTRASTIVE PIVOT — defining a thing by what it is not, or balancing it against a counter-claim in the same breath. "It's not just X, it's Y." "More than just a [noun]." "A working kitchen rather than a monument." "Not X, but Y." "More X than Y." Bare "X, not Y" where Y is abstract or metaphorical ("its own cuisine, not a hyphenated footnote"). "Feels both X and Y." "Deceptively simple." The shape itself is the tell — rewording the metaphor does not fix it. State the thing directly and drop the negation.

THE KICKER THAT IMPLIES A PAYOFF — a closer that gestures at a reason instead of giving it, leaving the reader to fill in the blank. "The line forms early for a reason." "The seating to chase." "Lower-key than the price suggests." "...which is why the 1pm seating fills first." "Special-occasion territory." State the actual reason, name the thing plainly, or cut the sentence.

Also banned, individually:
- "quietly [adjective]" (quietly radical, quietly confident, quietly stunning)
- "what happens when X meets Y" or "where X meets Y" or "the space between X and Y" — any phrasing that names an abstract interaction between two ingredients, techniques, or cultures instead of describing the result. Describe the result, not the interaction.
- "in a world where..."
- "the [noun] is [verb]-ing" sweeping openers (the city is changing, the menu is evolving)
- "a masterclass in"
- "punches above its weight"
- "the kind of [noun] that..."
- "effortlessly [adjective]"
- "the most X you can Y" or "the X-est you can Y" superlative-of-experience ("the tightest fish you can eat in the city"). The shape sounds writerly and commits to nothing concrete. State what the place actually does, or cut the claim.
- "set the bar," "raise the bar," "move the needle"
- "speaks volumes," "speaks to"
- "at its core," "at the heart of"
- "testament to"
- Compound mood adjectives of the form "[noun]-forward" or "[noun]-led" used to describe a room or program ("art-forward," "produce-forward"). Name the thing instead.
- Strained-clever metaphors that sound good on first read and empty on second ("earn its seat at the table," "writes its own chapter"). If you cannot say the thing literally, do not say it figuratively.
- Two-clause aphoristic closer with abstract nouns — short balanced clauses joined by semicolon, "and," or a comma, with both clauses ending in an abstract or metaphorical noun ("The room is the draw, and the food is the proof."). The parallel-with-abstract-noun shape is a strong signal even when each clause would be fine alone. Cut the symmetry or rewrite as two sentences with different shapes.
- Clipped imperative sign-offs as a closer, whether they end the paragraph or trail a compound sentence as the second clause ("Book weeks out, ideally more." / "Go hungry."). Covers Book, Reserve, Order, Skip, Arrive, Sit, Come, Bring, Go, Stay, Treat. Either fold the practical note into a full sentence earlier, or drop it.
- Any sentence ending in a tidy summary that restates the paragraph.

Banned personifications. Menus do not move, dance, weave, sing, or whisper. Rooms do not breathe. Flavors do not converse. Dishes do not "do the talking," "carry the conversation," "speak for themselves," "make the case," or "argue." Food is not an orator. Cut all of these.

No em dashes, and no substitutes for them. A comma-bracketed aside is an em dash in disguise: if you would have written "X — Y — Z", do not write "X, Y, Z" instead. Asides like "arguing, convincingly, that" or "the room is warm, and quietly so, throughout" get rewritten as one sentence with a subordinate clause, or as two shorter sentences, or dropped. Reach for the subordinate clause first: "the room is warm throughout, which is what makes the terrace worth booking" keeps the thought whole and needs no dash. Splitting is the last resort, not the house style. None of this bans long sentences: commas joining clauses are correct and wanted, and what is banned is a comma standing in for a dash around an aside. A spaced hyphen is the same dash in another hat and reads as a typewriter artefact.

Ration hyphenated compounds: roughly one per 200 words, so about four or five in a full article. It is a budget and not a ban. Spend it where the hyphen is the word rather than a shortcut — "stir-fried" is what the dish is, and "cooked quickly in a wok" is a worse sentence written to dodge a rule. What the budget exists to stop is the stack: "a well-known, family-run spot near two-bedroom apartments on a long-stay visa" is one of the clearest signals the text was generated, and every one of those is a modifier that could have been a phrase. Rephrase those: "apartments with two bedrooms", "a visa for long stays", "a spot the family runs, and people know it". Dates and measures are the usual offenders and count the same — "19th-century", "six-month", "10-kilometer". Proper names are free: "Aix-en-Provence" costs nothing.

Rhythm rules. Vary sentence length aggressively. Clustering at ANY length is the failure: sentences all sitting between 9 and 14 words read as generated just as surely as all sitting between 15 and 25. Every section carries at least one sentence under 8 words and at least one over 25, and three in a row within five words of each other means the next one breaks the pattern hard.

Length comes from subordination, not punctuation. Join clauses with because, which, while, after, so that, and with relative pronouns. Where one fact explains another, carry both in one sentence instead of lining them up one per full stop.

Parallel structure ("A and B, C and D") is fine once per paragraph, never twice. Do not end paragraphs with a balanced two-clause summary line.

Specificity rules. Every paragraph should contain at least one of: a proper noun beyond the subject, a number, a named dish or object, a date or year, a direct quote, or a physical detail that could only come from being there (a smell, a texture, an awkward moment, a small failure) — IF the source material supports it. Do not invent facts to satisfy this rule. If the source is thin on anchors, prefer a shorter paragraph or merge with an adjacent one rather than inventing a dish name, price, year, or quote. Generalizations without anchors are the strongest AI signal, but fabricated anchors are worse.

Banned hedges and softeners. Cut: arguably, perhaps, somewhat, rather, quite, fairly, genuinely, truly, really, simply, just, of course, indeed. Cut "it's worth noting that," "it's important to remember," and any meta-commentary about the writing itself.

Banned disclaimers. Never write about the enquiry. The reader is here for the place, not for how we found out about it. State what you know as a plain fact and stop: "Customs took twenty five minutes" is the whole sentence. Do not caveat a fact, attribute it defensively, date it as a shield, or explain how it was established.

Four moves are banned, in every wording.

1. Telling the reader how much to trust a claim. Cut: "based on my own experience," "anecdotally," "at the time of writing," "your experience may vary," "this is one traveller's experience," "this is not an average," and any sentence whose job is to tell the reader how much to trust the previous one.

2. Narrating a gap. Cut: "no official figures exist for," "there is no public data on," "figures could not be verified," "does not publish," "has not disclosed," "is not public information," "is not publicly available," "could not be confirmed." Where research could not establish something, write around it: never narrate the gap. Write what the subject does do, or say nothing.

3. Letting the vocabulary of the research onto the page. No "sampled" booking flows or menus, no "data points," no "sample size," no "evidence records," and no grading your own confidence in a number ("an estimate rather than a guaranteed bill"). Give the number plainly or leave it out.

4. Putting a publication between you and the claim. Cut: "sources report," "travel sources," "outlets anticipate," "one outlet," "the publication noted," "the report cited," "according to," "reports suggest." A named person or institution who acts in the story stays; the outlet that wrote it up does not.

This bans hedging, not first person. In a piece written in first person, "I waited twenty five minutes at customs" is the fact, told plainly, and it stays. A date or a season belongs in the prose when the reader needs it to act — a closure, a season, a change to the place itself — never as armour around a claim. Accuracy is settled before the writing starts; it is not the reader's problem.

Banned summary patterns. Do not open with a thesis sentence and close with a restated thesis. Do not write "in conclusion," "ultimately," "all in all," or any equivalent. End on a concrete detail or a specific recommendation, not a sweeping verdict.

Banned adjective stacking. No three-adjective lists ("warm, unfussy, and inviting"). Pick one adjective and make it earn its place, or replace the adjective with a noun or verb that shows the same thing.

Banned superlatives without anchors. Do not write "the smartest / sharpest / finest / deepest / tightest / cleanest / leanest / most thoughtful / most considered / most committed [wine list, sake program, cellar, beverage program, by-the-glass, tasting menu, room, kitchen, pairing, cocktail program]" without immediately naming the specific feature that earns the claim. "Runs one of the smartest wine and sake programs on the continent" is empty unless the next clause names the producers stocked, the by-the-glass policy, the markup, the format, or a named sommelier choice. If the source material does not support a specific anchor, drop the superlative and describe the program with a concrete noun instead. Vague evaluative superlatives are the structural opposite of editorial judgment — they sound confident and commit to nothing.

Diction rules. Prefer short Anglo-Saxon words over Latinate ones — "use" not "utilize," "show" not "demonstrate," "about" not "regarding." Cut "leverage," "curate," "craft" (as a verb), "elevate," "showcase," "highlight," "navigate" (when not literal).

Voice rules. Write from a single point of view with an opinion. If the writing could have been produced by a committee that has never been to the place, rewrite it. Take a side. Risk being wrong. AI prose is recognizable partly because it never commits — every claim is balanced against its counter-claim within the same sentence.

Final test. Read the draft as if aloud. If it sounds like every other piece of competent writing on the internet, it is AI prose. The fix is almost always more specificity and less symmetry.

Catalog file; applies only if selected by the relevant stage. Source: apps/backend/data/prompt2blog/forms/analysis.md

Catalog / forms/analysis.md
---
id: analysis
label: Analysis
summary: Answers a real question about a place and commits to the answer.
order: 2
opening: form-led
sections: 3-12
payoff: answer
closing: form-led
---

## Use when

Use when the reader has a question with a real answer and wants it settled — is Lisbon actually getting more expensive, has the diving recovered, is the night train worth it over the flight. The grill establishes this: the operator was asked whether they wanted a guide or wanted to make the case, and said the case. Analysis needs one subject, one bounded question, and enough evidence to answer it rather than describe around it.

## Do not use when

Do not use when the operator asked for a guide, an orientation, or a plan — this form is unreachable except through the grill's own question, and a model may not select it from a title. Use News Report for a timely event, Explainer where the reader needs understanding rather than a verdict, or Comparison when weighing two subjects is the promise.

## Reader promise

Answer the question the reader actually has, and commit to the answer. Say what the answer costs them — what it changes about where they go, what they book, what they pay. A reader who finishes this should be able to act, not merely to summarise both sides.

## Required evidence

Require current, relevant evidence for every load-bearing claim, and enough context to judge change over time. Define the baseline, period, geography and measurement behind words like affordable, safer, busier or declining. Where indicators genuinely conflict, say which one you believe and why, rather than averaging them into a shrug. Context-only places may calibrate a point but never become co-subjects or sections.

## Allowed structures

1. The answer, then what makes it true, then what would change it.
2. What changed, why it changed, and who it changes things for.
3. The common belief, what the evidence actually shows, and what to do about it.

Organise around the question and the subject, never around the research that answered it. No section may take scope, limits, method, or the state of the evidence as its subject.

## Failure modes

Avoid thesis drift, cherry-picking, vague trend language, and causal claims from correlation. Do not hedge the answer into uselessness — a qualified answer names the one thing that qualifies it, in a clause, and moves on. Do not widen a single-city question into a three-city comparison. Do not write about the enquiry: the reader came for the place, not for how we found out.

## Headline note

Name the finding, not the investigation. "Lima's best food is at the market" is a headline; "What the evidence says about Lima's food scene" is a filing label. A question is acceptable only when the article answers it plainly.

Catalog file; applies only if selected by the relevant stage. Source: apps/backend/data/prompt2blog/forms/comparison.md

Catalog / forms/comparison.md
---
id: comparison
label: Comparison
summary: Evaluates approved co-subjects against consistent criteria for a defined choice.
order: 12
opening: direct-answer
sections: 3-12
payoff: decision
closing: takeaways
---

## Use when

Use only when the commission explicitly approves `head_to_head` or `ranked_set` scope and names every comparator. The reader must face a real choice, and the criteria must reflect that reader’s priorities.

## Do not use when

Do not use because another place appears as context, a benchmark, or a source example. A `single_subject` commission cannot become Comparison. Use Analysis when one primary subject is being tested and other places merely calibrate evidence.

## Reader promise

Compare like with like, show meaningful differences, explain tradeoffs, and help the primary audience choose without pretending one answer fits everyone. Preserve the approved comparator set and roles.

## Required evidence

Require comparable evidence for every subject and load-bearing criterion. Align periods, currencies, geographic units, service levels, and definitions. Explain conversions and methodological mismatches. Current evidence for one subject cannot be paired silently with old or anecdotal evidence for another. State where comparison is impossible or confidence differs.

## Allowed structures

1. Reader decision, criteria, criterion-by-criterion comparison, best fit by scenario.
2. Short subject profiles, shared scorecard in prose, tradeoffs, qualified verdict.
3. Ranked set with disclosed weighting, evidence notes, and alternatives by priority.

Organize around criteria, not separate promotional mini-guides, unless short profiles are required for orientation.

## Failure modes

Avoid false equivalence, shifting criteria, hidden weighting, universal winners, cherry-picked prices, and expanding the comparator set during research or writing. Context-only references never receive equal sections or verdicts. Missing comparable evidence must remain a visible gap.

## Headline note

Name the approved subjects and decision. “Versus” is appropriate only for true head-to-head scope. Do not imply a decisive winner when the result depends on reader priorities.

Catalog file; applies only if selected by the relevant stage. Source: apps/backend/data/prompt2blog/forms/cost-budget-breakdown.md

Catalog / forms/cost-budget-breakdown.md
---
id: cost-budget-breakdown
label: "Cost & Budget Breakdown"
summary: Builds a dated, transparent budget from defined assumptions and sourced costs.
order: 15
opening: direct-answer
sections: 3-12
payoff: decision
closing: takeaways
---

## Use when

Use when the commission’s main promise is what a trip, stay, move, or activity costs. Define destination, period, duration, party size, travel style, currency, and inclusions. This form may model several realistic budgets without ranking destinations.

## Do not use when

Do not use for general affordability commentary, a service choice, or a multi-place value contest. Use Analysis, Service Guide, or Comparison. A few price examples do not constitute a budget breakdown.

## Reader promise

Show where money goes, what assumptions drive totals, which costs are fixed or variable, and where readers can adjust. Give ranges and scenarios when precision would mislead.

## Required evidence

Source every material price or calculation input. Record currency, tax and fee treatment, unit, booking or observation date, travel period, and conversion date. Distinguish advertised prices, typical observed prices, averages, medians, and estimates. Show arithmetic or enough inputs to reproduce totals. Include irregular costs only when the commission defines them.

## Allowed structures

1. Assumptions, category breakdown, daily and total scenarios, savings levers, uncertainty.
2. Fixed costs, variable costs, sample budgets by travel style, sensitivity check.
3. One realistic budget diary, category analysis, alternative scenarios, planning range.

Keep categories mutually understandable and avoid double counting. Explain whether transport to the destination is included.

## Failure modes

Avoid false precision, silent currency conversion, mixing dates or service levels, cherry-picked bargain prices, unsupported “average” claims, and presenting a promotional rate as normal. Never fabricate bridge values to complete a total; report a gap or partial estimate.

## Headline note

Name destination or task, duration, audience when relevant, and the pricing period. Use a number only when its assumptions are visible and current.

Catalog file; applies only if selected by the relevant stage. Source: apps/backend/data/prompt2blog/forms/curated-list-best-of.md

Catalog / forms/curated-list-best-of.md
---
id: curated-list-best-of
label: Curated List/Best Of
summary: Selects and explains a bounded set of options using explicit editorial criteria.
order: 11
opening: direct-answer
sections: 3-12
payoff: decision
closing: takeaways
---

## Use when

Use when selection is the reader value: the best museums for families, notable neighborhood restaurants, worthwhile day trips, or a short set of places matching a defined need. The commission must bound geography, audience, category, and selection criteria.

## Do not use when

Do not use for an unranked destination inventory, a provider directory, or a comparison requiring a single winner. Use Destination Guide, Service Guide, or Comparison. Do not call a list “best” when evidence only establishes popularity or existence.

## Reader promise

Offer a defensible, useful shortlist. Explain why every item belongs, who it suits, meaningful tradeoffs, and current practical details. The list should reduce choice, not reproduce search results.

## Required evidence

Verify identity, location, current operation, relevant offerings, access, and any stated price or booking requirement. Use evidence appropriate to the selection criteria; popularity rankings cannot establish quality by themselves. Disclose whether the list is ranked, alphabetical, geographic, or thematic. Keep inclusion standards consistent across items and identify material evidence gaps.

## Allowed structures

1. Selection method, ranked entries, best-for labels, practical comparison, decision shortcut.
2. Thematic groups, concise entries, tradeoffs, map or route logic in prose.
3. Unranked editor’s picks, each tied to one explicit reader need, followed by choosing advice.

Item count should follow evidence and reader utility, never a predetermined SEO number.

## Failure modes

Avoid arbitrary rankings, repetitive descriptions, unsupported superlatives, affiliate-style product language, and entries included only to reach a number. Do not mix categories with incompatible criteria. Never invent a visit, meal, or evaluation.

## Headline note

Name category, place, and audience or criterion. Use a number only when final inventory is stable. “Best” requires stated editorial judgment; otherwise prefer “worthwhile,” “notable,” or a direct category label.

Catalog file; applies only if selected by the relevant stage. Source: apps/backend/data/prompt2blog/forms/destination-guide.md

Catalog / forms/destination-guide.md
---
id: destination-guide
label: Destination Guide
summary: Gives a coherent planning overview of one approved destination.
order: 8
opening: direct-answer
sections: 3-12
payoff: decision
closing: takeaways
---

## Use when

Use when readers need broad orientation to a destination before or during a visit. The commission must bound the geography and traveler context. A destination guide may connect neighborhoods, timing, transport, costs, customs, and major experiences without becoming an exhaustive encyclopedia.

## Do not use when

Do not use for a single practical problem, a day-by-day plan, or a ranked list. Use Service Guide, Itinerary, or Curated List/Best Of. Do not use when the title asks a narrow analytical question.

## Reader promise

Help the primary audience understand the destination, make core planning decisions, avoid consequential mistakes, and know what deserves further research. Maintain the named destination as the primary subject throughout.

## Required evidence

Verify entry basics, local movement, meaningful geographic distinctions, timing, closures, and safety or cost claims included by the commission. Prefer official and current sources for changeable facts. Explain who a recommendation suits and its tradeoffs. Context-only places may orient readers but cannot become parallel guide sections.

## Allowed structures

1. Orientation, when to go, where to base, what to experience, logistics, practical cautions.
2. Key planning decisions, area guide, daily rhythms, transport, budget, responsible travel.
3. First-visit priorities, destination layout, booking decisions, common mistakes, next steps.

Choose sections from the approved modules and requirements. Do not force every travel topic into every guide.

## Failure modes

Avoid generic praise, exhaustive attraction inventories, timeless claims about changing details, unsupported superlatives, and advice without traveler fit. Do not flatten distinct neighborhoods or cultures into stereotypes. Flag missing operational facts instead of filling them with plausible travel copy.

## Headline note

Name the bounded destination and planning promise. Add audience, season, or trip context only when central. Avoid “ultimate” and “complete” unless the scope truly warrants them.

Catalog file; applies only if selected by the relevant stage. Source: apps/backend/data/prompt2blog/forms/explainer.md

Catalog / forms/explainer.md
---
id: explainer
label: Explainer
summary: Makes a complex system, rule, event, or travel concept understandable.
order: 3
opening: direct-answer
sections: 3-12
payoff: answer
closing: takeaways
---

## Use when

Use when readers need a clear mental model before they can act or form a view. Suitable subjects include visa systems, transit networks, tourism rules, pricing mechanisms, local customs, environmental events, or unfamiliar industry terms.

## Do not use when

Do not use for breaking developments whose timing is the main value, personal advocacy, or a step-by-step task. Use News Report, Opinion/Column, or How-To/Checklist instead. If the commission asks whether a proposition remains true, use Analysis.

## Reader promise

Answer what the subject is, how it works, why it exists, whom it affects, and where exceptions apply. Define every necessary term before relying on it. Leave readers able to interpret future information without memorizing the article.

## Required evidence

Prefer official rules, primary documentation, subject-matter specialists, and strong explanatory reporting. Verify jurisdiction, eligibility, dates, thresholds, and exceptions. Use examples to illuminate rules, not replace them. When authorities disagree or implementation differs from written policy, label both and explain the evidentiary limit.

## Allowed structures

1. Short answer, key terms, mechanism, example, exceptions, practical meaning.
2. Reader misconception, accurate model, component-by-component explanation, implications.
3. Timeline or process map followed by the rules that govern each stage.

Choose the smallest structure that makes the system coherent. Use questions as subheads only when they match real reader questions.

## Failure modes

Avoid circular definitions, unexplained acronyms, fake simplicity, generic history, and long procedural detours. Do not convert estimates into guarantees or jurisdiction-specific rules into universal advice. Never invent an exception to make the explanation feel complete; mark the gap.

## Headline note

Name the exact concept and reader benefit. “How X works” is useful when mechanism is central. Avoid inflated claims such as “the complete guide” for a bounded explanation.

Catalog file; applies only if selected by the relevant stage. Source: apps/backend/data/prompt2blog/forms/feature-profile.md

Catalog / forms/feature-profile.md
---
id: feature-profile
label: Feature/Profile
summary: Builds a reported narrative around a person, place, community, or phenomenon.
order: 4
opening: form-led
sections: 3-12
payoff: insight
closing: form-led
source_gate: reported-people-scenes-quotations
---

## Use when

Use when the commission promises character, scene, observation, and reported depth rather than a reference guide. A profile centers a person or group; a feature may center a place, practice, enterprise, or cultural change while still relying on human voices and concrete scenes.

## Do not use when

Do not use when research contains only generic web summaries, no attributable voices, or no observed or documented scenes. Use Explainer or Analysis if evidence is principally documentary. Do not fabricate color to imitate magazine writing.

## Reader promise

Bring readers close to the approved subject while explaining its wider significance. Specific people, moments, places, and quotations should reveal the story. Narrative detail must remain factual and attributed.

## Required evidence

Require supplied interviews, transcripts, field notes, firsthand material, or sufficiently detailed reported sources supporting every promised person, scene, and quotation. Identify who observed each scene and when. Verify biographical facts, chronology, roles, and relevant context independently where possible. Composite characters, invented dialogue, imagined thoughts, reconstructed sensory detail, and unattributed quotations are prohibited.

## Allowed structures

1. Defining scene, subject background, central tension, reported development, resonant return.
2. Profile portrait, formative history, present work, stakes, outside perspective.
3. Thematic feature moving among two or three reported scenes, with context between them.

Narrative structure cannot broaden the commission’s primary subject. Secondary voices provide perspective, not competing profiles, unless explicitly approved.

## Failure modes

Avoid hero worship, promotional biography, decorative quotations, invented interiority, chronology confusion, and scenes assembled from unrelated facts. Do not claim representativeness from one person. If promised access, quotations, or scenes are missing, stop with a research gap.

## Headline note

Prefer the subject’s name or defining tension over generic inspiration language. A feature headline may be evocative, but its deck or opening must quickly establish the factual subject.

Catalog file; applies only if selected by the relevant stage. Source: apps/backend/data/prompt2blog/forms/how-to-checklist.md

Catalog / forms/how-to-checklist.md
---
id: how-to-checklist
label: How-To/Checklist
summary: Guides readers through a bounded task with verified steps and checkpoints.
order: 14
opening: direct-answer
sections: 3-12
payoff: decision
closing: takeaways
---

## Use when

Use when the reader needs to complete a specific task: apply, book, pack, configure, prepare, submit, transfer, or verify. The commission should identify the starting state, successful end state, audience, jurisdiction or destination, and important constraints.

## Do not use when

Do not use for conceptual understanding, broad planning, or a choice among many services. Use Explainer, Destination Guide, or Service Guide. A checklist alone is not a substitute for missing procedural evidence.

## Reader promise

Provide a reliable sequence, required inputs, decision points, warnings, and completion check. Readers should know what to prepare, what to do, what can fail, and how to confirm success.

## Required evidence

Use current official instructions or primary operator documentation for mandatory steps, forms, fees, deadlines, and eligibility. Verify links, names, order, and jurisdiction. Supplement with specialist or firsthand evidence only for practical friction, not to override authoritative requirements. Identify effective and retrieval dates. Mark optional steps and paths that vary by reader.

## Allowed structures

1. Before you start, numbered steps, troubleshooting, completion check.
2. Checklist grouped by timing: weeks before, day before, day of, after.
3. Decision tree with separate verified paths, then a shared final check.

Keep each step atomic and outcome-focused. Place warnings immediately before the risky action.

## Failure modes

Avoid missing prerequisites, vague verbs, mixed jurisdictions, obsolete screenshots or labels, hidden fees, and false guarantees. Do not invent a workaround. If one critical step cannot be verified, expose the gap rather than publishing a broken sequence.

## Headline note

Lead with the task and relevant place, system, or deadline. “Step by step” is useful only when the article contains a genuine ordered process.

Catalog file; applies only if selected by the relevant stage. Source: apps/backend/data/prompt2blog/forms/interview-qa.md

Catalog / forms/interview-qa.md
---
id: interview-qa
label: Interview/Q&A
summary: Presents attributable answers from a named interview around a focused reader question.
order: 5
opening: form-led
sections: 2-12
payoff: answer
closing: form-led
source_gate: attributable-responses
---

## Use when

Use when the interview itself is the editorial value and the commission names a qualified speaker, subject, and focus. It may be a lightly edited transcript or a concise introduction followed by selected questions and answers.

## Do not use when

Do not use without a transcript, recording, written responses, or another supplied record of attributable answers. Do not generate answers from a person’s public statements or imitate their voice. Use Feature/Profile for a reported portrait or Explainer for synthesized expertise.

## Reader promise

Let readers hear a real person answer coherent, relevant questions. Preserve meaning, distinctive voice, qualifications, and uncertainty while removing only material that is genuinely repetitive or unclear.

## Required evidence

Require the speaker’s name, role, interview date, interview method, and attributable response record. Every answer must trace to that record. Fact-check material claims and flag corrections or editor’s notes transparently. Disclose editing for length or clarity. Never merge separate answers without indicating the edit, invent connective phrases, or convert paraphrase into quotation.

## Allowed structures

1. Brief introduction, edited Q&A, closing context or resources.
2. Short factual setup, thematic groups of questions, final practical answer.
3. Selected Q&A excerpts with clearly labeled editorial context between groups.

Questions may be reordered for comprehension if chronology is not distorted. Preserve important caveats near the claims they qualify.

## Failure modes

Avoid flattering setup, repetitive softball questions, answers stripped of conditions, hidden paraphrase, and anonymous expertise. Do not insert answers to unasked questions. If required responses are absent or attribution is uncertain, report a research gap instead of completing the piece.

## Headline note

Name the speaker and the central subject. Quoted headline language must appear exactly in the attributable record. Avoid implying exclusivity unless documented.

Catalog file; applies only if selected by the relevant stage. Source: apps/backend/data/prompt2blog/forms/itinerary.md

Catalog / forms/itinerary.md
---
id: itinerary
label: Itinerary
summary: Sequences a realistic trip plan across an approved time window and geography.
order: 10
opening: direct-answer
sections: 3-12
payoff: decision
closing: takeaways
---

## Use when

Use when the reader wants a day-by-day or stop-by-stop plan. The commission must specify destination, duration, primary audience, pace, and important constraints such as arrival time, mobility, budget, opening days, or transport mode.

## Do not use when

Do not use for a loose list of attractions, a destination overview, or a route that lacks evidence for timing and feasibility. Use Curated List/Best Of or Destination Guide instead. Do not fabricate a schedule from approximate distances.

## Reader promise

Provide a coherent plan that a real person could follow, with sensible grouping, travel time, recovery time, booking needs, and alternatives. Explain why each stop belongs and what can be dropped.

## Required evidence

Verify opening schedules, reservation requirements, seasonal access, travel times, route connections, and geographic order. Use current official sources for operational details and mapping or operator evidence for movement. Mark estimates and variability. Respect meal times, check-in constraints, daylight, altitude, weather, accessibility, and weekly closures when relevant.

## Allowed structures

1. Day-by-day plan with morning, afternoon, evening, logistics, and optional swap.
2. Base-and-excursion plan grouped by geography, with arrival and departure days.
3. Stop-by-stop route with duration ranges, transfer notes, and contingency branches.

Sequence comes from feasibility and reader priorities, not from source order or venue popularity.

## Failure modes

Avoid impossible transfers, overpacked days, unexplained backtracking, exact minute schedules without support, and treating optional stops as mandatory. Do not hide booking or mobility barriers. If critical operational facts are missing, return a research gap instead of a plausible itinerary.

## Headline note

State destination and duration. Add pace or audience only when it materially distinguishes the plan. Avoid “perfect itinerary”; travel conditions vary.

Catalog file; applies only if selected by the relevant stage. Source: apps/backend/data/prompt2blog/forms/news-report.md

Catalog / forms/news-report.md
---
id: news-report
label: News Report
summary: Reports a timely development, what changed, and what readers should know now.
order: 1
opening: direct-answer
sections: 2-12
payoff: answer
closing: form-led
---

## Use when

Use for a specific, recent development whose timing matters: a route launch, policy change, closure, opening, disruption, court ruling, public warning, or other verifiable event. The commission should identify the event, affected people, location, and publication moment.

## Do not use when

Do not use for evergreen advice, speculative trend pieces, or broad destination summaries. If the event only supplies a hook for a deeper argument, use Analysis. If readers mainly need background, use Explainer.

## Reader promise

State what happened, when, where, who is affected, why it matters, and what remains uncertain. Separate confirmed facts from claims, projections, and reaction. Make the newest verified information easy to find.

## Required evidence

Require at least one authoritative or firsthand source for the central event, plus independent reporting or documentation when available. The evidence record preserves timestamps, effective dates, jurisdiction, named speakers, and quotation attribution. Named people and institutions who act in the story are the story and stay in the prose; the outlet that reported it does not. For an evolving story, identify the reporting cutoff. Never turn an announcement into an accomplished fact.

## Allowed structures

1. News lead, verified details, impact, background, next developments.
2. What changed, who is affected, practical consequences, unanswered questions.
3. Chronology of a fast-moving event, followed by current status and reader action.

Keep background subordinate to the news. Use chronological order only when it clarifies cause or changing facts.

## Failure modes

Avoid stale present-tense claims, buried dates, anonymous authority, invented reaction, false balance, promotional framing, and predictions presented as outcomes. Do not pad thin news with generic destination copy. Flag conflicts and unknowns plainly.

## Headline note

Name the development and affected place or group. Use a date only when it prevents ambiguity. Avoid “everything you need to know” unless the report genuinely covers the full practical impact.

Catalog file; applies only if selected by the relevant stage. Source: apps/backend/data/prompt2blog/forms/opinion-column.md

Catalog / forms/opinion-column.md
---
id: opinion-column
label: Opinion/Column
summary: Advances a clearly identified viewpoint using evidence and transparent reasoning.
order: 6
opening: form-led
sections: 2-12
payoff: insight
closing: form-led
---

## Use when

Use when the commission asks an author to argue a position, interpret experience, or recommend a change. The viewpoint, authorial standing, intended audience, and claim under debate should be explicit.

## Do not use when

Do not use to launder unsupported assertions as analysis, manufacture controversy, or mimic a person’s beliefs. Use Analysis when the publication’s evidence-led judgment is central and Personal Essay/Travelogue when lived experience supplies the main arc.

## Reader promise

Offer a distinct, intelligible position; show how the author reached it; engage the strongest fair objection; and distinguish value judgments from verifiable facts. Readers should understand the reasoning even if they disagree.

## Required evidence

Support factual premises with appropriate sources. Identify the author’s relevant experience, interests, or limitations when material. Represent opposing evidence accurately and in context. Personal observation may support a viewpoint but cannot establish broad prevalence on its own. Never invent public sentiment, motives, or a convenient opponent.

## Allowed structures

1. Position, stakes, evidence, strongest counterargument, response, conclusion.
2. Concrete incident, broader principle, supporting cases, proposed action.
3. Common assumption, author’s disagreement, evidence and limits, alternative view.

Keep the approved proposition stable. Contextual comparisons may illustrate reasoning but cannot turn into an unapproved ranked or head-to-head article.

## Failure modes

Avoid ranting, false dilemmas, selective facts, straw arguments, moral certainty unsupported by evidence, and calls to action disconnected from the case. Do not conceal a recommendation inside neutral language. Do not present preference as universal traveler truth.

## Headline note

Signal the position or tension honestly. First person is acceptable when it clarifies authorship. Avoid rage-bait, claims about what “everyone” thinks, and questions the column never answers.

id: personal-essay-travelogue

## Use when

Use when a real journey, encounter, or personal change is the primary material and the author has supplied notes, memories, journals, photographs, recordings, or a draft. The commission should identify the experience and the insight it may illuminate without predetermining a false lesson.

## Do not use when

Do not use if no first-person material exists, the writer would need to impersonate an experience, or practical advice is the true purpose. Use Destination Guide or Service Guide for reader planning, Feature/Profile for reported narrative, or Opinion/Column for argument.

## Reader promise

Give readers an honest, specific account with a meaningful reflective arc. Sensory detail, dialogue, chronology, emotion, and uncertainty must come from supplied material rather than invention.

## Required evidence

Require attributable firsthand material for every scene, quotation, sequence, and personal claim. External sources may verify place, history, or practical context, but they cannot manufacture lived experience. Preserve uncertainty where memory is incomplete. Protect private people through approved anonymization without creating composite events or characters. Distinguish what the author observed, inferred, and later learned.

## Allowed structures

1. Opening scene, journey or encounter, turning point, reflective return.
2. Chronological travelogue with selected moments and a restrained conclusion.
3. Braided essay alternating documented experience with carefully sourced context.

Select scenes for the approved insight, not merely itinerary completeness. Practical context should support the narrative, not replace it.

## Failure modes

Avoid invented dialogue, false epiphany, tourist-as-hero framing, exoticism, compressed timelines presented literally, and universal claims drawn from one trip. Do not add danger, romance, or sensory detail for drama. Missing firsthand support requires a research gap.

## Headline note

Favor a concrete image, journey, or honest realization. First person is acceptable. Avoid claiming transformation or revelation stronger than the supplied account supports.

## Use when

Use when the commission asks for an editorial judgment based on a real evaluation. The subject, evaluator, date, method, audience, and criteria should be known. Reviews may cover lodging, tours, transport products, restaurants, attractions, or travel equipment.

## Do not use when

Do not use from marketing copy, aggregated ratings, or general web research alone. Do not imply firsthand use where none exists. Use Service Guide for choosing among documented options or Feature/Profile for a reported subject.

## Reader promise

Tell readers what was evaluated, under what conditions, what worked, what failed, who it suits, and whether it delivers reasonable value. Separate observed performance from published specifications and third-party claims.

## Required evidence

Require firsthand notes or a documented evaluation record attributable to the reviewer. Record date, version or offering, price paid or provided access, conditions, and relevant limitations. Verify specifications, policies, and current public pricing independently. Disclose complimentary access, affiliate interest, or unusual treatment. Never invent testing, sensory experience, staff interaction, durability, or long-term performance.

## Allowed structures

1. Verdict, evaluation context, strengths, weaknesses, value, best fit.
2. Experience chronology, criterion-based assessment, alternatives, conclusion.
3. What was promised, what was observed, practical drawbacks, recommendation by audience.

Apply the same declared criteria throughout. Comparisons to alternatives remain contextual unless approved as a Comparison commission.

## Failure modes

Avoid promotional recap, star ratings without a rubric, universal recommendations, recency ambiguity, and treating one visit as permanent truth. Do not omit material failures or disclosure. If the evaluation record cannot support the promised judgment, stop with a research gap.

## Headline note

Name the exact subject and useful verdict or question. Avoid “honest review,” which should be assumed, and avoid claims of testing duration not documented in evidence.

## Use when

Use for a bounded service question such as choosing an airport transfer, using a rail pass, finding accessible lodging, arranging connectivity, or navigating a booking rule. The commission should name the reader, decision, location, and practical outcome.

## Do not use when

Do not use for an overview of an entire destination, a strict sequence of actions, or a ranked product list. Use Destination Guide, How-To/Checklist, or Curated List/Best Of. Use Explainer when understanding the system matters more than making a choice.

## Reader promise

Give the reader enough verified information to choose, book, use, or avoid a service confidently. State tradeoffs, eligibility, timing, costs, and failure points in terms relevant to the primary audience.

## Required evidence

Use official operator or authority sources for routes, rules, schedules, eligibility, and published prices. Add independent reporting or firsthand specialist evidence for reliability, usability, and real-world friction. Capture currency, tax or fee inclusion, effective dates, booking windows, cancellation rules, and accessibility limits when relevant. Never infer availability from an outdated listing.

## Allowed structures

1. Quick recommendation, option breakdown, decision factors, booking or use instructions, cautions.
2. Reader scenario, available services, tradeoff table in prose, best fit by need, fallback plan.
3. Before arrival, at point of use, troubleshooting, alternatives.

Organize around the approved decision, not around providers’ marketing categories.

## Failure modes

Avoid generic tips, undisclosed sponsored framing, price claims without dates, absolute reliability claims, and recommendations with no audience fit. Do not silently treat missing operational detail as unchanged. If a critical rule or availability claim cannot be verified, expose the gap.

## Headline note

Name the task or decision, location, and meaningful constraint. Prefer specific utility over “best way” unless evidence supports one best choice for the stated audience.

# Prompt2Blog house rules

## Brief fidelity

Preserve the approved brief: location, spine, primary subject, scope mode, reference roles, and everything under must name. Answer the core reader question and deliver the promised outcome. Context-only references may calibrate a fact or explain significance; they cannot become co-subjects, recurring sections, rankings, or verdicts. Do not change form because source material suggests another article.

## Evidence discipline

Use only claims the facts you were given support. Preserve their meaning, dates, geography, units, and stated uncertainty. Attribution is internal to the evidence record: the prose never names a source, outlet, publication, or site. Never invent a bridge fact, scene, quotation, experience, statistic, price, consensus, or practical detail. A point the evidence does not support is left out of the article — not hedged, not labelled unconfirmed, not narrated as something research could not establish. Prefer a narrower true article over a complete-looking unsupported one.

## Reader service

Write for the named primary audience. Explain unfamiliar terms before relying on them. Make constraints, tradeoffs, dates, exceptions, and consequential actions easy to find. Audience tags adjust emphasis; they do not dictate structure or justify stereotypes.

## Prose

Use direct, specific language and varied, readable paragraphs. Lead sections with meaning, not throat-clearing. Avoid generic travel praise, repeated conclusions, fake scene-setting, clichés, “hidden gem,” “vibrant tapestry,” and claims that a place has “something for everyone.” Use lists only when sequence or comparison benefits.

## Safety and fairness

Do not overstate medical, legal, financial, immigration, safety, accessibility, or environmental advice. Identify the deciding authority and limits. Describe people and communities precisely, without exoticism or treating one voice as representative. State a limit that changes what the reader should do; a material conflict the evidence leaves unsettled is not written as settled.

## Research questions

Which areas fit the primary audience, and why? What are the tradeoffs in access, atmosphere, noise, mobility, cost, and daily needs? What lodging types, restrictions, booking patterns, or seasonal pressures matter? Are named boundaries official, customary, or platform-defined?

## Preferred sources

Use municipal maps and planning sources, official lodging rules, transport authorities, current operator or property information, reputable local reporting, and attributable firsthand evidence. Booking platforms may show examples but not prove typical prices or neighborhood character.

## Freshness

Verify current operation, rules, transit access, and material price claims. Neighborhood history may use older sources; practical recommendations need recent support.

## Factual limits and gaps

Avoid declaring an area universally best, safe, authentic, quiet, or walkable. State audience fit and tradeoffs. Do not flatten disputed boundaries or infer lived conditions from listings. Warn when accommodation legality, accessibility, operational status, or a load-bearing neighborhood claim cannot be verified.

## Research questions

What route, activity, environment, duration, skill, fitness, guide, permit, equipment, and emergency plan are required? Which seasonal, altitude, wildlife, water, fire, or weather conditions affect feasibility? What lower-risk alternatives fit the audience?

## Preferred sources

Use park and land authorities, route managers, rescue and weather agencies, licensed operators, recognized outdoor bodies, current maps, and attributable firsthand reports. Commercial descriptions cannot establish safety or route status alone.

## Freshness

Verify permits, access, trail or water conditions, closures, operator status, and warnings close to publication. Clearly date condition-dependent evidence.

## Factual limits and gaps

Do not declare an activity easy, safe, family-friendly, or suitable for beginners without defined conditions. Never invent route detail or substitute generic preparation advice for local evidence. Warn when access, rescue coverage, required experience, guide rules, or a load-bearing condition report is missing.

## Research questions

What costs matter to the primary audience? What period, geography, currency, unit, party size, and standard of service make figures comparable? Which costs changed, and what explains the change? Does “affordable” mean low absolute price, value for quality, or affordability relative to income?

## Preferred sources

Use official tariffs, operator prices, government statistics, reputable market datasets, dated menus or booking evidence, and methodologically transparent reporting. Use firsthand observations as examples, not market averages.

## Freshness

Treat prices, exchange rates, rents, and fees as volatile. Record observation and conversion dates. Older trend series may establish direction but cannot substitute for a current planning figure.

## Factual limits and gaps

Never mix currencies, periods, neighborhoods, taxes, or service levels silently. Label advertised, observed, average, median, and modeled figures accurately. Do not infer a citywide cost from one listing. Warn when essential categories lack current evidence, samples are not comparable, or a claimed bargain depends on an exceptional rate.

## Research questions

Which behavior, setting, community, language, ceremony, or historical context matters to the commission? What varies by generation, region, faith, relationship, or formality? What should a visitor ask, observe, avoid, or reciprocate rather than assume?

## Preferred sources

Use local scholars, cultural institutions, community organizations, language authorities, reputable local reporting, and attributable local or firsthand voices. Tourism marketing may identify topics but should not define cultural truth alone.

## Freshness

Historical context can be durable; current terminology, laws, contested practices, community preferences, and event protocols require recent verification.

## Factual limits and gaps

Avoid universal claims about what locals think, authenticity tests, exoticism, and etiquette lists detached from context. Distinguish legal requirements, formal protocol, common courtesy, and one person’s preference. Warn when the commission promises community perspective without attributable voices or when a contested claim has only one institutional viewpoint.

## Research questions

What dishes, drinks, markets, producers, customs, or venues answer the commission? What makes them relevant to this audience? Which claims concern history, identity, quality, price, dietary fit, reservation, or current operation?

## Preferred sources

Use official venue information for hours and policies, menus for dated price examples, food authorities, producers, scholars, reputable culinary reporting, and attributable firsthand material for taste or service judgments. Aggregated reviews can reveal questions, not establish facts alone.

## Freshness

Recheck operation, chef or ownership claims, menus, prices, reservations, and opening schedules. Cultural and historical claims still require credible sourcing even when less volatile.

## Factual limits and gaps

Never claim the writer tasted, visited, or experienced something without supplied firsthand evidence. Avoid “authentic,” “best,” and origin stories without definition and support. Note dietary cross-contact uncertainty. Warn when venue status, a quoted price, attribution, or a promised firsthand evaluation is missing.

## Research questions

Who may stay, for how long, and under what work conditions? What housing, connectivity, workspace, banking, tax, insurance, healthcare, time-zone, community, and daily-life constraints matter? Which claims apply to visitors, residents, employees, contractors, or dependants?

## Preferred sources

Use immigration and tax authorities, official labor guidance, telecom data, housing rules, healthcare sources, reputable market research, and attributable long-stay experience. Forums may reveal research questions but cannot settle legal or typical-cost claims.

## Freshness

Recheck visas, remote-work permissions, tax thresholds, rental rules, connectivity products, and prices. Date market and speed evidence.

## Factual limits and gaps

Do not give individualized legal or tax advice, equate visa permission with work authorization, or infer citywide livability from one neighborhood. Separate published internet speed from usable service. Warn when work legality, tax exposure, housing assumptions, healthcare access, or current connectivity evidence remains unresolved.

## Research questions

What hazards are relevant to the approved place, activity, time, and audience? What is the likelihood, severity, and practical mitigation? Which risks vary by neighborhood, season, transport mode, identity, health status, or behavior? What can official evidence establish, and what remains uncertain?

## Preferred sources

Use local authorities, emergency and health agencies, official advisories, methodologically sound crime or incident data, transport operators, specialist safety bodies, and careful local reporting. Firsthand accounts illustrate conditions but cannot establish prevalence.

## Freshness

Verify alerts, closures, health guidance, laws, and operational risks near publication. Historical data needs dates, definitions, and geographic fit.

## Factual limits and gaps

Never label a whole city or neighborhood safe or unsafe without qualification. Avoid fearmongering, reassurance beyond evidence, and cross-city crime comparisons built from incompatible data. Give actionable precautions without blaming victims. Warn when promised risk comparisons, emergency details, or claims about safer areas lack comparable support.

## Research questions

Which months, elevations, microclimates, events, or activities matter? What are typical ranges, rainfall patterns, daylight, extreme-weather risks, crowd cycles, closures, and price effects? How much year-to-year variability should readers expect?

## Preferred sources

Use national meteorological agencies, climate normals, park or destination authorities, disaster agencies, event organizers, operators, and reputable local reporting. Forecasts support imminent conditions, not general seasonal claims.

## Freshness

Use an appropriate climate-normal period and identify it. Recheck current seasonal closures, event dates, active warnings, and anomalous conditions close to publication.

## Factual limits and gaps

Do not promise weather, call one month universally best, or confuse climate averages with forecasts. Distinguish coast, valley, mountain, and neighborhood conditions where meaningful. Warn when activity access depends on unverified conditions, event dates are unsettled, or cited averages do not fit the approved geography.

## Research questions

Which journey or network must readers navigate? What routes, transfers, operating windows, fares, payment methods, booking rules, luggage limits, and accessibility conditions matter? How do options differ in time, cost, reliability, comfort, and risk for the primary audience?

## Preferred sources

Prefer transport authorities, operators, airports, official maps and timetables, accessibility documentation, and current service notices. Use reputable local reporting or attributable firsthand evidence for recurring friction and real-world usability.

## Freshness

Treat schedules, fares, routes, construction, strikes, payment systems, and entry procedures as volatile. Record effective or retrieval dates and account for day-of-week or seasonal differences.

## Factual limits and gaps

Do not convert scheduled time into guaranteed journey time or one trip into a reliability rate. Separate official rules from observed enforcement. Warn when a critical connection, fare, accessibility feature, safety condition, or current operating status cannot be verified.

## Research questions

Which passport, residence status, travel purpose, destination, transit point, and intended stay apply? Is a visa, authorization, insurance, onward ticket, registration, fee, or minimum passport validity required? Which authority decides, and where can the traveler verify before departure?

## Preferred sources

Use destination immigration authorities, embassies or consulates, foreign ministries, official application portals, and carrier documentation for boarding requirements. Specialist reporting may explain implementation but cannot override official rules.

## Freshness

Entry rules are highly volatile. Verify immediately before publication, preserve effective and retrieval dates, and link readers to the deciding authority.

## Factual limits and gaps

Never generalize one nationality’s rules to another, promise admission, or present anecdotal enforcement as policy. Distinguish visa exemption, visa on arrival, electronic authorization, and permission to work. Warn when nationality-specific eligibility, transit rules, fees, or the official source cannot be confirmed.
